questions.stem: A 55-year-old man presents to the emergency department with sudden chest pain radiating to his left arm and jaw. His electrocardiogram shows ST-segment elevation, and laboratory studies indicate elevated cardiac biomarkers. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management for this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 55-year-old man presents to the emergency department with sudden chest pain radiating to his left arm and jaw. His electrocardiogram shows ST-segment elevation, and laboratory studies indicate elevated cardiac biomarkers. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management for this patient?

options.label: D
options.text: Medical management with antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy

questions.solution: Correct Option B- Percutaneous Coronary Intervention: This patient presents with acute ST-segment elevation myocardial Infarction (STEMI), which requires immediate reperfusion therapy. Percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) is the preferred initial treatment for STEMI when performed within 90 minutes of presentation. PCI involves the insertion of a catheter into the blocked artery to open the occlusion, allowing blood flow to the heart muscle. PCI is more effective than thrombolytic therapy in improving outcomes in STEMI patients. Incorrect Options: Option A- Coronary Artery Bypass Graft Surgery: Coronary artery bypass graft surgery (CABG) is an option for patients with severe and extensive coronary artery disease that cannot be treated with PCI. CABG is not the initial management for acute STEMI and is usually reserved for stable patients with chronic stable angina or unstable angina. Indications of CABG are as follows: High-grade left main stem coronary artery stenosis Significant stenosis (>70%) of the proximal left anterior descending artery, with 2-vessel or 3-vessel disease Symptomatic 2-vessel or 3-vessel disease Disabling angina despite maximal medical therapy Poor left ventricular function with myocardium that can return to function on revascularization Post Infarct angina Indications for emergency CABG Non-ST segment elevation myocardial infarction with ongoing ischemia that is unresponsive to medical therapy/PCI STEMI with inadequate response to all nonsurgical therapy Significant ongoing ischemia, traumatic complications, or threatened occlusion in STEMI, after a failed PCI or previous CABG. Option C- Thrombolytic therapy: Thrombolytic therapy involves administering drugs to dissolve the clot causing coronary artery occlusion. Thrombolytic therapy is an alternative to PCI in STEMI patients who present within 12 hours of symptom onset and cannot undergo PCI within 120 minutes. However, thrombolytic therapy has a higher risk of bleeding complications than PCI and is less effective in restoring blood flow to the heart muscle. Option D- Medical management with antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy: Medical management with antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy is a component of the initial management for STEMI patients but is not the definite treatment for acute STEMI. These medications may stabilize the patient and prevent further clot formation while awaiting PCI or thrombolytic therapy. @Neet_pg_bot

  • Percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) is the preferred initial treatment for STEMI when performed within 90 minutes of presentation. 
  • PCI involves the insertion of a catheter into the blocked artery to open the occlusion, allowing blood flow to the heart muscle. 
  • PCI is more effective than thrombolytic therapy in improving outcomes in STEMI patients.

Incorrect Options: 

Option A- Coronary Artery Bypass Graft Surgery:

  • Coronary artery bypass graft surgery (CABG) is an option for patients with severe and extensive coronary artery disease that cannot be treated with PCI. 
  • CABG is not the initial management for acute STEMI and is usually reserved for stable patients with chronic stable angina or unstable angina.
    • Indications of CABG are as follows:
      • High-grade left main stem coronary artery stenosis
      • Significant stenosis (>70%) of the proximal left anterior descending artery, with 2-vessel or 3-vessel disease
      • Symptomatic 2-vessel or 3-vessel disease
      • Disabling angina despite maximal medical therapy
      • Poor left ventricular function with myocardium that can return to function on revascularization
      • Post Infarct angina
    • Indications for emergency CABG 
      • Non-ST segment elevation myocardial infarction with ongoing ischemia that is unresponsive to medical therapy/PCI
      • STEMI with inadequate response to all nonsurgical therapy
      • Significant ongoing ischemia, traumatic complications, or threatened occlusion in STEMI, after a failed PCI or previous CABG.

Option C- Thrombolytic therapy:

  • Thrombolytic therapy involves administering drugs to dissolve the clot causing coronary artery occlusion. 
  • Thrombolytic therapy is an alternative to PCI in STEMI patients who present within 12 hours of symptom onset and cannot undergo PCI within 120 minutes. 
  • However, thrombolytic therapy has a higher risk of bleeding complications than PCI and is less effective in restoring blood flow to the heart muscle.

Option D- Medical management with antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy:

  • Medical management with antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy is a component of the initial management for STEMI patients but is not the definite treatment for acute STEMI.
  • These medications may stabilize the patient and prevent further clot formation while awaiting PCI or thrombolytic therapy.

questions.stem: A 49-year-old gentleman k/c/o CML on imatinib for 3 years, presents to the ER with complaints of shortness of breath. Work-up reveals WBC of 90,000/µL , hemoglobin 8.9 g/dL, and platelets of 119,000/µL. Review of the peripheral smear reveals that he has at least 30% blasts. Flow cytometry reveals that he has acute myeloid leukemia. Bone marrow biopsy confirmed that he now has transformation to AML, with 35% blasts. Molecular studies show that he has detectable BCR-ABL p210 transcripts. Cytogenetics are sent. Mutation analysis does not reveal a new activating mutation. What is the ideal mode of management?
questions.stemHtml: A 49-year-old gentleman k/c/o CML on imatinib for 3 years, presents to the ER with complaints of shortness of breath. Work-up reveals WBC of 90,000/µL , hemoglobin 8.9 g/dL, and platelets of 119,000/µL. Review of the peripheral smear reveals that he has at least 30% blasts. Flow cytometry reveals that he has acute myeloid leukemia. Bone marrow biopsy confirmed that he now has transformation to AML, with 35% blasts. Molecular studies show that he has detectable BCR-ABL p210 transcripts. Cytogenetics are sent. Mutation analysis does not reveal a new activating mutation. What is the ideal mode of management?

options.label: C
options.text: Change to second generation tyrosine kinase inhibitor , provide supportive care and wait to assess response.

questions.solution: Correct Option D- Daunorubicin plus cytarabine plus imatinib: The patient's presentation and clinical course suggest that he has transformed from chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) to acute myeloid leukemia (AML) in blast crisis. Blast crisis is an aggressive transformation of CML where the disease shifts from a chronic phase to an acute leukemia-like phase. In this phase, there is a rapid increase in the number of immature myeloid cells (blasts) in the bone marrow and peripheral blood. The management approach for a patient with CML in blast crisis involves combining treatment strategies for both AML and CML. This means using intensive chemotherapy to induce remission in the AML component, while also targeting the underlying CML with tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) to reduce the BCR-ABL activity. Daunorubicin plus cytarabine plus imatinib, reflects this combined approach. Daunorubicin and cytarabine are standard chemotherapy agents used in the induction regimen for AML.Imatinib, which is a first-generation TKI targeting BCR-ABL, is included to continue controlling the underlying CML component. This combined treatment aims to achieve remission . Incorrect Options: Option A- "HyperCVAD + imatinib": HyperCVAD is a chemotherapy regimen commonly used in the treatment of acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) but is not typically employed as a first-line treatment for AML. Moreover, since the patient already has CML with evidence of blast crisis, using only HyperCVAD would not adequately address the underlying CML component, and imatinib alone might not be sufficient to manage the disease. Option B- "Daunorubicin plus cytarabine": This choice involves the standard induction chemotherapy for AML, but it lacks the targeting of the BCR-ABL abnormality seen in CML. Given the patient's history of CML, it's important to continue TKI therapy like imatinib to address both aspects of the disease. Option C- "Change to second generation tyrosine kinase inhibitor, provide supportive care and wait to assess response": While switching to a second-generation TKI might be considered in CML management, this choice does not address the acute myeloid transformation (AML) which is the primary concern at this point. Waiting to assess response without initiating appropriate treatment for AML can lead to disease progression and worsen the patient's condition. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 43-year-old woman is found to have iron deficiency anemia. A colonoscopy is normal to the terminal ileum. An upper endoscopy is performed and she is found to have a thin horizontal membrane protruding from the anterior wall in the upper esophagus and mid esophagus. What is a person with this condition at increased risk for?
questions.stemHtml:
A 43-year-old woman is found to have iron deficiency anemia. A colonoscopy is normal to the terminal ileum. An upper endoscopy is performed and she is found to have a thin horizontal membrane protruding from the anterior wall in the upper esophagus and mid esophagus.
What is a person with this condition at increased risk for?

options.label: A
options.text: Squamous cell carcinoma of the pharynx

questions.answerText: Squamous cell carcinoma of the pharynx
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Squamous cell carcinoma of the pharynx: The syndrome characterized by iron deficiency anemia, dysphagia, and cervical esophageal webs is known as Plummer-Vinson syndrome. This syndrome identified a group of patients at increased risk for squamous cell cancer of the esophagus and pharynx. Incorrect Options: Option B - Adenocarcinoma of the esophagus: This option is incorrect because Plummer-Vinson syndrome is associated with an increased risk of squamous cell carcinoma of the esophagus and pharynx, not adenocarcinoma. Adenocarcinoma of the esophagus is commonly associated with Barrett's esophagus, a condition where the normal lining of the esophagus is replaced by abnormal cells, usually due to chronic gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD). Option C - Peptic stricture: This option is incorrect because Peptic strictures are not associated with Plummer-Vinson syndrome. Peptic strictures are caused by chronic inflammation and scarring from long-term acid reflux and are most commonly seen in the lower part of the esophagus. Option D - Eosinophilic esophagitis: This option is incorrect because Eosinophilic esophagitis is a chronic allergic inflammatory condition of the esophagus that leads to symptoms like difficulty swallowing, food impaction, and heartburn. It is not directly associated with Plummer-Vinson syndrome, which primarily presents with iron deficiency anemia, dysphagia, and esophageal webs. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Which of the following is correct about SPINK1?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following is correct about SPINK1?

options.label: A
options.text: It is considered a susceptibility gene in the development of chronic pancreatitis

questions.solution: Correct Option B - It inhibits trypsin autoactivation: SPINK1 acts as the first line of defense against prematurely activated trypsinogen in the acinar cell and inhibits trypsin autoactivation. It is considered a modifier gene, rather than a susceptibility gene. A mutation affecting SPINK1 does not by itself increase the risk of pancreatic disease. However, in someone with a PRSS1 mutation, the presence of an additional SPINK1 mutation strongly drives the pancreatic injury and resultant fibrosis. CFTR l, not SPINK1, leads to trypsin flushing into the duodenum. CTRC leads to trypsin degradation Incorrect Options: Option A - It is considered a susceptibility gene in the development of chronic pancreatitis: This option is incorrect. In contrast to this statement, Option A is actually correct. SPINK1 gene mutations or variants are considered a susceptibility gene in the development of chronic pancreatitis. Mutations in the SPINK1 gene can lead to reduced inhibition of trypsin, increasing the risk of trypsin activation and autodigestion of the pancreas, which is a key factor in the development of chronic pancreatitis. Option C - It inhibits CFTR: This option is incorrect. SPINK1 does not inhibit CFTR (Cystic Fibrosis Transmembrane Conductance Regulator). CFTR is a different gene that is associated with cystic fibrosis, a genetic disorder that affects various organs, including the lungs, pancreas, and digestive system. SPINK1 is not directly related to CFTR or cystic fibrosis. Option D - It enhances trypsin degradation: This option is incorrect. SPINK1 inhibits trypsin autoactivation rather than enhancing trypsin degradation. By inhibiting trypsin, SPINK1 helps prevent the premature activation of trypsin in the pancreas, which could lead to pancreatitis. Enhancing trypsin degradation is not one of SPINK1's known functions. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: You are seeing a patient with advanced ER/PR+ Her2- breast cancer. Due to relapse with ddAC/T, she then was on SERD + CDK4/6 for 2 years, and then had progression. She has mild CKD, CTP A cirrhosis, diabetes and poorly controlled hypertension. Which of her comorbidities would disqualify her from a combination of ixabepilone + capecitabine?
questions.stemHtml: You are seeing a patient with advanced ER/PR+ Her2- breast cancer. Due to relapse with ddAC/T, she then was on SERD + CDK4/6 for 2 years, and then had progression. She has mild CKD, CTP A cirrhosis, diabetes and poorly controlled hypertension. Which of her comorbidities would disqualify her from a combination of ixabepilone + capecitabine?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Cirrhosis The patient's cirrhosis, specifically Child-Pugh Class A, indicates a mild form of liver disease, which would impair the liver's ability to metabolize drugs like ixabepilone and capecitabine. This could lead to increased drug levels in the blood, causing a higher incidence of adverse effects, such as neutropenia-related sepsis. The liver's role in drug metabolism and the elevated risk of adverse effects in patients with liver disease make cirrhosis a contraindication for the use of ixabepilone + capecitabine. Incorrect Options: Option B - Diabetes: Diabetes does not generally contraindicate the use of ixabepilone and capecitabine. The metabolism and clearance of these drugs do not rely on insulin or glucose levels. However, diabetes might indirectly affect the patient's overall health and tolerance to treatment, so close monitoring would be needed. Option C - Hypertension: While hypertension should be well-controlled before initiating any chemotherapy due to potential cardiovascular risk, it is not a specific contraindication for the use of ixabepilone and capecitabine. Option D - CKD (Chronic Kidney Disease): Mild CKD does not contraindicate the use of ixabepilone and capecitabine, as these drugs are primarily metabolized in the liver. However, in severe renal impairment, capecitabine use should be avoided due to an increased risk of adverse reactions. As this patient has only mild CKD, it is not a contraindication for this combination therapy. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: An 18-month-old female presents with 6 days of fever and dry cough. The child is up-to-date on her vaccinations and is otherwise healthy. Her temperature is 101.1 degrees. Physical examination is remarkable for red dry lips, a strawberry tongue, cervical lymphadenopathy, a rash on her perineum, and erythema of the palms and feet. What is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient?
questions.stemHtml: An 18-month-old female presents with 6 days of fever and dry cough. The child is up-to-date on her vaccinations and is otherwise healthy. Her temperature is 101.1 degrees. Physical examination is remarkable for red dry lips, a strawberry tongue, cervical lymphadenopathy, a rash on her perineum, and erythema of the palms and feet. What is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient?

options.label: D
options.text: Rapid strep test and lumbar puncture

questions.solution: Correct Option B - Aspirin and intravenous immune globulin: This patient has Kawasaki disease , a vasculitis of small and medium blood vessels with an unknown cause. Treatment is with high dose aspirin and intravenous immune globulin (IVIG). Complications include dysrhythmias, myocardial infarction and coronary artery aneurysms . Incorrect Options: Option A - Antipyretics, antibiotics, and close follow-up: Patients with Kawasaki disease (KD) should be admitted and started on aspirin. Antibiotics are not indicated in patients with KD. Option C - Plasmapheresis: Plasmapheresis has no role in the treatment of KD Option D - Rapid strep test and lumbar puncture: A lumbar puncture is not indicated in patients with KD. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Which of the following is a characteristic of tumour suppressor genes?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following is a characteristic of tumour suppressor genes?

options.label: A
options.text: The mutant allele is often inherited through the germ line

options.label: B
options.text: The somatic mutation does not contribute to cancer

options.label: C
options.text: The inherited form of the mutant allele does not commonly have a tissue preference

options.label: D
options.text: The mutant allele acts in a dominant fashion

questions.answerText: The mutant allele is often inherited through the germ line
questions.solution: Correct Option A - The mutant allele is often inherited through the germ line Unlike oncogenes, tumour suppressor genes are commonly inherited through the germ line. The only known example of an oncogene being inherited due to a dominant germline mutation in a proto-oncogene is the RET oncogene, which leads to multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 (MEN2). Oncogenes act as gain of function mutations and require only one mutation, while tumour suppressor genes generally function as loss of function mutations and require two mutations. Incorrect Options: Option B - The somatic mutation does not contribute to cancer: Somatic mutations in tumor suppressor genes can indeed contribute to cancer development. Somatic mutations are acquired during an individual's lifetime and occur in non-germline cells, such as somatic cells of the body. These mutations can lead to the loss of function of tumor suppressor genes, which, in turn, can result in uncontrolled cell growth and the development of cancer. Inactivation of tumor suppressor genes in somatic cells is a common event in various cancers. Option C - The inherited form of the mutant allele does not commonly have a tissue preference: The inherited form of the mutant allele in some tumor suppressor genes can indeed show a tissue preference or predisposition for specific types of cancer. For example, individuals with germline mutations in the BRCA1 or BRCA2 tumor suppressor genes have a higher risk of developing breast and ovarian cancers. Similarly, individuals with germline mutations in the APC gene have an increased risk of developing colorectal cancer. Option D - The mutant allele acts in a dominant fashion: Tumor suppressor genes typically act in a recessive fashion at the cellular level. This means that both copies (alleles) of the tumor suppressor gene must be inactivated or lost to contribute to the development of cancer. Inherited germline mutations in tumor suppressor genes increase the risk of cancer development, but it usually requires a second "hit" or somatic mutation in the remaining allele to cause complete loss of function and lead to cancer. The loss of both alleles is usually required for the manifestation of malignancy at the cellular level, even though the inheritance pattern at the organismal level may be autosomal dominant. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option B- Tetralogy of Fallot: Aortic and pulmonary outflows are separated by an infundibular septum and its anterior deviation during the development results in the Tetralogy of Fallot which is characterized by the following four abnormalities. Pulmonary stenosis leading to right ventricular outflow obstruction. Ventricular septal defect. Hypertrophy of the right ventricle. Ventricular septum is overridden by the aorta due to its dextroposition. The right atrium and ventricle venous return is normal but the contraction of the right ventricle shunts blood to the left ventricle through VSD due to pulmonary stenosis. Cyanosis results due to the desaturation of the blood. Symptoms like right ventricular hypertrophy and cyanosis severity depends on the degree of right ventricular outflow tract obstruction. Cyanosis is noted in infants with severe obstruction. In mild degrees of obstruction, infants may initially have signs of heart failure but cyanosis occurs in the first few months as the right ventricular infundibulum hypertrophies with time. Incorrect Options: Option A- Ventricular septal defect: The membranous ventricular septal defect that occurs on the anterior side of the septal leaflet of the tricuspid valve in the posteroinferior position is the most common type although the defect can also occur in the muscular region of the septum. Patients with small lesions are mostly asymptomatic and at the left lower sternal border a loud harsh murmur often associated with a thrill can be heard during regular physical examination. Option C- Transposition of great vessels: It is a cyanotic cardiac abnormality in which blood normally returns to the left atrium through pulmonary veins and blood from systemic veins returns to the right atrium but the aorta arises from the right ventricle and pulmonary artery from the left ventricle. The left side of the heart receives oxygenated blood from the pulmonary veins and it is then transferred again to the lungs. The right side of the heart receives deoxygenated blood from the body and it is returned to the body through the aorta. Option D- Truncus arteriosus: In this condition, due to failure of aorticopulmonary septal development truncus arteriosus fails to divide into the aorta and pulmonary trunk, and a single arterial trunk supplies pulmonary and systemic circulations. Initial findings in the neonatal period are cyanosis and a murmur over the next few months torrential pulmonary blood flow develops, and heart failure becomes prominent. Her blood pressure is 90/60 mmHg, pulse is 120 bpm and respiratory rate is 30 breaths per minute. Her oxygen saturation is 88% on room air. A pulmonary embolism is detected on CT angiography. The patient has no contraindications for thrombolysis. What is the most appropriate initial therapy for this patient?

questions.solution: Correct Option B- Tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) infusion: The clinical presentation of this patient is consistent with pulmonary thromboembolism. Pulmonary thromboembolism (PTE) is a potentially life-threatening condition that occurs when a blood clot blocks one or more pulmonary arteries. The clinical presentation of PTE includes dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, hemoptysis, tachypnea, tachycardia, and hypoxia. The patient's presentation is a medical emergency and requires prompt diagnosis and management. The most appropriate initial therapy for this patient is tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) infusion. Thrombolysis with tPA is a recommended treatment for patients with PTE who are hemodynamically unstable or have evidence of right ventricular dysfunction. The use of tPA for PTE is supported by several clinical trials that have demonstrated improved mortality and morbidity outcomes compared to anticoagulation alone. Incorrect Options: Option A- Heparin infusion: Heparin infusion is an appropriate initial therapy for patients with PTE who are hemodynamically stable. Anticoagulation with heparin is recommended as the first-line therapy for most patients with PTE, and it should be started as soon as the diagnosis is made. However, in hemodynamically unstable patients, thrombolysis with tPA is preferred over anticoagulation alone. Option C- Surgical embolectomy: Surgical embolectomy is an appropriate therapy for patients with massive PTE who are hemodynamically unstable and not responding to thrombolysis. However, surgical embolectomy is associated with a higher risk of morbidity and mortality compared to thrombolysis. It should only be considered if the patient's condition does not improve with thrombolysis. Option D- Inferior vena cava filter placement: Inferior vena cava filter placement is an appropriate therapy for patients with contraindications to anticoagulation or in whom anticoagulation has failed. It is not the most appropriate initial therapy for this patient, as she has no contraindications for thrombolysis and is hemodynamically unstable. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stemHtml: What is the best indicator that an ICU is a highly reliable organization?

options.label: A
options.text: ICU bed can be requested at any time

questions.answerText: There is no significant change in mortality, despite increased volume
questions.solution: Correct Option B - There is no significant change in mortality, despite increased volume. The High-Reliability Organization is most often described as an organization that performs high-risk work but rarely experiences catastrophic events. Hospitals are only one type of such an organization. The term was devised initially to strengthen ICUs by combining several levels of care from patient safety to staff satisfaction. This organization can adapt to large shifts of volume without decreasing its performance. Incorrect Options: Option A - ICU bed can be requested at any time: The availability of ICU beds at any time does not necessarily indicate that the ICU is a highly reliable organization. While it is essential to have sufficient bed capacity to meet the needs of critically ill patients, the availability of beds alone does not guarantee the overall reliability and quality of care provided by the ICU. Option C - Leadership of ICU is recognized at the national level: While having recognized leadership at the national level can be a positive aspect of an ICU, it does not directly indicate that the ICU is a highly reliable organization. Leadership recognition may be based on various factors, including research contributions, academic achievements, or involvement in professional organizations. While these are commendable accomplishments, they may not directly reflect the day-to-day operational reliability of the ICU. Option D - ICU physician provides critical care consultations throughout the hospital: While providing critical care consultations throughout the hospital is an essential service that can improve patient care and outcomes, it does not alone signify that the ICU is a highly reliable organization. Reliability in healthcare organizations encompasses a broader range of factors, including patient safety, effective teamwork, communication, protocols, and quality improvement initiatives. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option B - Patients are at an elevated risk of developing squamous cell carcinoma: This statement is not accurate. Therefore, statement B is the correct answer as it is not true in the context of SDS Incorrect Options: Option A - By age 30 up to 35% of patients will have developed either MDS or AML: This statement is true. The cited statistic emphasizes the substantial risk these patients face, especially by age 30. The majority of patients with SDS will present with malabsorption symptoms early in life due to the lack of pancreatic enzymes needed to digest food, particularly fats. questions.stem: A 72-year-old male is admitted to the ICU for aspergillosis. Liposomal amphotericin B is ordered. Shortly after the infusion, the patient develops chills, a fever, and diffuse muscle pain. His vital signs are stable, and the infusion is continued. A day later, the patient experiences anuria. What is the most plausible reason for his anuria?
questions.stemHtml: A 72-year-old male is admitted to the ICU for aspergillosis. Liposomal amphotericin B is ordered. Shortly after the infusion, the patient develops chills, a fever, and diffuse muscle pain. His vital signs are stable, and the infusion is continued. A day later, the patient experiences anuria. What is the most plausible reason for his anuria?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Renal ischemia: Amphotericin is a highly nephrotoxic medication. The mechanism of toxicity is related to enhanced renal tubuloglomerular feedback, leading to vasoconstriction of the renal arteriole and ischemia. This causes irreversible renal ischemia and subsequent renal failure. A liposomal modification of amphotericin B has a slightly lower nephrotoxic profile than the original drug formulation. Liposomal amphotericin is also preferred to treat central nervous infections due to a slightly better penetration. Incorrect Options: Option B – Rhabdomyolysis: These symptoms may suggest rhabdomyolysis, but direct amphotericin nephrotoxicity is more likely. They are typical side effects of the infusion of the drug and can be alleviated, at least partially, by diphenhydramine, acetaminophen, and hydrocortisone. Occasionally, these symptoms force a break in the therapy. Option C – Dehydration: This patient was just admitted. He has no history of prior low fluid intake. Option D - Tubular obstruction: Tubular obstruction is a related complication in patients receiving acyclovir. Low circulating volume, incorrect dosing, and rapid infusion are conducive to the formation of crystals in the tubule of the nephron and subsequent renal failure. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option A- Dilatation of coronary vessels: Dipyridamole is a phosphodiesterase type 3 inhibitor used for treating coronary stent restenosis and intermittent vascular claudication and as an antiplatelet (anti-angina, TIA/stroke prevention) drug. Dipyridamole induces coronary vasodilation by raising adenosine levels and activating adenosine A2A receptors. Myocardial ischemia brought on by a shift of blood flow is known as coronary steal syndrome. The seriously stenotic arteries' rigidity only permits a small coronary flow reserve. Blood is therefore directed to collaterals and healthy vessels when coronary arteries widen. As a result, there is tissue ischemia distal to the coronary artery stenosis , which causes chest tightness and novel ECG abnormalities. The adenosine or dipyridamole pharmacological stress test is based on this occurrence. Incorrect Options: Option B- Increased myocardial oxygen demand: The dobutamine stress test and the cardiac exercise stress test increase myocardial oxygen demand (MVO2). Dipyridamole influences myocardial oxygenation and coronary perfusion but has minimal effects on MVO2. Option C- Vasospasm of coronary arteries: The ECG changes observed in this patient's case would be caused by the vasospasm of coronary arteries , which is the source of Prinzmetal angina. However, unlike this patient, who complained of chest tightness with exertion, Prinzmetal angina patients usually experience symptoms at rest. Dipyridamole treatment, which causes vasodilation rather than vasospasm but also causes chest pain, indicates a different reason for this patient's symptoms. Option D- Ruptured atherosclerotic plaque within coronary vessels: The mechanism that causes acute coronary syndrome (ACS), which would result in chest tightness and the ECG changes observed here, is thrombotic occlusion of a coronary vessel after the rupture of a cholesterol plaque. Every stress test carries some risk for ACS, but the risk is minimal with a dipyridamole stress test because the drug prevents platelet coagulation. A different cause probably brought on chest tightness in this patient. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Which of the following best characterizes restrictive lung diseases, such as pulmonary fibrosis?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following best characterizes restrictive lung diseases, such as pulmonary fibrosis?

options.label: A
options.text: Both FEV and FVC are reduced, but characteristically the FEV1.0/FVC% is normal or increased

options.label: B
options.text: The FEV1.0 is reduced much more than the FVC, giving a low FEV/FVC%

options.label: C
options.text: Reduction of the forced expiratory flow rate, or FEF 25-75%

options.label: D
options.text: The total lung capacity is increased to about 120%

questions.answerText: Both FEV and FVC are reduced, but characteristically the FEV1.0/FVC% is normal or increased
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Both FEV and FVC are reduced, but characteristically the FEV1.0/FVC% is normal or increased: In restrictive lung disease, such as pulmonary fibrosis, both FEV and FVC are reduced, but characteristically the FEV1.0/FVC% is normal or increased. Additional characteristics of restrictive lung disease include a total lung capacity which will be around 4 L or less. Incorrect Options: Option B - The FEV 1.0 is reduced much more than the FVC, giving a low FEV/FVC%: This characteristic is typical of obstructive lung diseases, not restrictive lung diseases like pulmonary fibrosis. In obstructive lung diseases, such as bronchial asthma or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), the airways are narrowed, leading to increased resistance to airflow. This results in a greater reduction in the forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1.0) compared to the forced vital capacity (FVC). As a result, the FEV1.0/FVC% ratio is reduced, often below the normal range. Option C - Reduction of the forced expiratory flow rate, or FEF 25-75%: The reduction of the forced expiratory flow rate between 25% and 75% of the FVC (FEF25-75%) is not a characteristic feature of restrictive lung diseases like pulmonary fibrosis. Instead, it is more commonly seen in obstructive lung diseases, where there is narrowing of the airways and reduced flow rates during the mid-portion of forced expiration. It can be an early indicator of early-stage COPD before other lung function indicators, such as FEV1.0, become abnormal. Option D - The total lung capacity is increased to about 120%: An increased total lung capacity to about 120% (around 6 liters) is a characteristic finding in obstructive lung diseases, not in restrictive lung diseases. In obstructive lung diseases, the increased total lung capacity is due to air trapping caused by difficulty in fully exhaling air from the lungs, leading to a higher volume of air remaining in the lungs after exhalation. In restrictive lung diseases, like pulmonary fibrosis, the total lung capacity is reduced to around 4 liters or less due to the limited expansion of the lungs caused by the fibrotic changes in the lung tissue. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 67-year-old female with a h/o mantle cell lymphoma, treated with BR + filgrastim, and then subsequently with R-CHOP plus PEG-filgrastim for progressive disease, now presents to your clinic, 4 years later with a diagnoses of t-MDS. Which is the most likely culprit?
questions.stemHtml: A 67-year-old female with a h/o mantle cell lymphoma, treated with BR + filgrastim, and then subsequently with R-CHOP plus PEG-filgrastim for progressive disease, now presents to your clinic, 4 years later with a diagnoses of t-MDS. Which is the most likely culprit?
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Filgrastim Therapy-related myelodysplastic syndrome (t-MDS) and acute myeloid leukemia (t-AML) are known complications of chemotherapy and radiation therapy used to treat various malignancies, including non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL). Filgrastim is a granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF) that is commonly used to reduce the risk of neutropenia (low white blood cell count) in patients receiving myelosuppressive chemotherapy, such as the regimens used to treat mantle cell lymphoma (e.g., BR and R-CHOP). While filgrastim can help prevent severe neutropenia, it has been associated with an increased risk of t-MDS and t-AML, especially when used in combination with certain chemotherapeutic agents. The SEER (Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results) database review mentioned in the answer supports the association between filgrastim and t-MDS in patients with NHL. The review found a 3.7% incidence of t-MDS/AML in NHL patients exposed to filgrastim but not PEG-filgrastim. Incorrect Options: Option A - Rituximab: Rituximab is a monoclonal antibody commonly used in the treatment of mantle cell lymphoma and other B-cell lymphomas. It is not directly associated with an increased risk of t-MDS. Option B - Bendamustine: Bendamustine is an alkylating agent used in the treatment of various lymphomas, including mantle cell lymphoma. While it can be associated with some adverse effects, it is not specifically linked to an increased risk of t-MDS. Option D - PEG-filgrastim: PEG-filgrastim is a long-acting form of filgrastim that is used to reduce the duration of neutropenia after chemotherapy. While t-MDS risk may be lower with PEG-filgrastim compared to regular filgrastim, it is still associated with some risk. The SEER database review mentioned in the correct answer did not specifically address the association of PEG-filgrastim with t-MDS, so it is not clear if PEG-filgrastim carries a similar risk. However, it is still important to consider the possibility of t-MDS in any patient who has received prior chemotherapy and presents with myelodysplastic syndrome or acute myeloid leukemia. @Neet_pg_bot

Which of the following findings on pulmonary function testing is associated with this condition?

questions.solution: Correct Option C - Decreased expiratory flow: This patient has a clinical presentation that is consistent with relapsing polychondritis marked by an autoimmune response to the cartilaginous structures. The primary areas of involvement are the auricular cartilage, nasal cartilage, laryngotracheobronchial cartilage, joint cartilage, and heart (usually valvular). Laryngotracheobronchial disease often takes the form of luminal narrowing and peritracheal inflammation. Chronic inflammation causes the destruction of the supportive matrix around the tracheobronchial tree, and collapse on expiration is exaggerated. The result of pulmonary flow loops is low flow on expiration. Tracheal and bronchial stent placements are often employed but are not always successful. Incorrect Options: Option A - Decreased diffusion of carbon monoxide (DLCO): Decreased DLCO is typically seen in conditions that disrupt the alveolar-capillary interface or decrease the surface area for gas exchange, such as pulmonary fibrosis and emphysema. In relapsing polychondritis, there is an autoimmune attack against cartilaginous structures, including the laryngotracheobronchial tree, but the alveolar-capillary interface is typically spared. Option B - Decreased total lung capacity (TLC): Conditions that cause decreased TLC are typically restrictive lung diseases that reduce lung compliance, such as pulmonary fibrosis and chest wall abnormalities. In relapsing polychondritis, there's typically no significant effect on the lung parenchyma itself, so TLC is not typically decreased. Option D - Increased forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1): FEV1 is the volume of air that can be forcibly exhaled from the lungs in the first second of a forced exhalation. An increased FEV1 is not typical of any specific disease and can be seen in certain conditions such as recovery from an acute asthma exacerbation or with the use of bronchodilators. In relapsing polychondritis, the disease process can lead to collapse of the tracheobronchial tree during expiration due to the destruction of the supportive cartilaginous matrix, leading to a decreased expiratory flow, not increased FEV1. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 41-year-old nurse with a history of migraine headaches and fibromyalgia presents for evaluation of recurrent episodes of abnormal speech. The events started 18 months ago and there was no clear trigger for the first event. She describes a sense of “extreme fatigue” at the onset, followed by an inability to find words while speaking resulting in “choppy speech.” With 50% of these episodes, she suffers from “complete paralysis” that always starts in her right leg and over 1-2 minutes moves to the right arm, and then spreads to the left arm and leg. She maintains consciousness through every event and is aware of everything going on around her. She can understand everything that is being said to her but when she tries to respond to questions her speech is “off.” At times during these events, it feels like “her body no longer belongs to her.” The symptoms persist for 2-3 hours before she returns to her prior baseline. They occur 3-4 times per month. There is no relationship between these events and her headaches. She tells you that her right leg is “not quite 100%” after suffering an episode earlier that day. During your exam, she develops a brief period of stuttering/stammering speech that persists for no longer than 20 seconds and resolves with reassurance. You also find that she generates no movement when you are testing right hip extension despite the presence of a normal gait while walking back to the exam room. When you test her left hip flexion you detect at least 4+/5 strength in the right hip extensors. She tends to drag the right leg when her gait is formally tested but the remainder of her exam, including reflexes, is normal. In the last 18 months, she has been seen by four different neurologists and has undergone four separate brain MRIs, all of which were reported to be normal. Which of the following diagnoses is most likely in this patient?

questions.stem: A 75-year-old man presents to the emergency room for dizziness and palpitations for the past hour. His pulse is 185/min, and his blood pressure is 100/52 mm Hg. An ECG shows a narrow-complex, regular tachycardia without P waves. A drug activates cardiac potassium channels and causes the transient atrioventricular block. Which of the following adverse effects is most likely to occur?
questions.stemHtml: A 75-year-old man presents to the emergency room for dizziness and palpitations for the past hour. His pulse is 185/min, and his blood pressure is 100/52 mm Hg. An ECG shows a narrow-complex, regular tachycardia without P waves. A drug activates cardiac potassium channels and causes the transient atrioventricular block. Which of the following adverse effects is most likely to occur?
questions.solution: Correct Option C- Chest pain: The patient has been given the antiarrhythmic drug adenosine . Chest pain is a common adverse effect in patients treated with adenosine. Adenosine causes a transient atrioventricular (AV) block by increasing potassium efflux from cells, which causes hyperpolarization, decreased calcium influx, and decreased levels of intracellular cAMP. The brief AV block (usually < 15 secs) can cause chest pain and a feeling of impending doom. Other side effects of adenosine include hypotension, flushing, bronchospasm, bradycardia, and nausea. Prolonged asystole is rare but also a potential complication. Theophylline and caffeine are adenosine receptor antagonists that can inhibit the effect of adenosine. Incorrect Options: Option A- Severe headache: This statement is incorrect as severe headache is a common side effect of nitrates (e.g., nitroglycerin, isosorbide dinitrate), which release nitric oxide in smooth muscle cells, resulting in vasodilation and increased intracranial pressure. Other side effects of nitrates include hypotension, reflex tachycardia, and syncope. Severe headaches are not a common side effect of adenosine, which this patient received. Option B- Sedation: This statement is incorrect as sedation is a known side effect of beta-blockers (e.g., metoprolol, labetalol) and class IB antiarrhythmics (e.g., lidocaine, mexiletine). These lipophilic agents can penetrate the blood-brain barrier, resulting in CNS side effects. Adenosine does not cause sedation. Option D- Dry cough: This statement is incorrect as adenosine does not cause dry cough. Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors can cause dry cough. @Neet_pg_bot

Brain MRI, particularly with diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) sequence, is highly sensitive and specific in detecting acute ischemic changes and can provide more detailed information about the location and extent of the stroke. questions.stemHtml: A 34-year-old woman presents to the doctor with complaints of missing her menstrual cycle for the past 4 months, despite having regular periods every 28 days with moderate flow. questions.solution: Correct Option B - Adenohypophysis: This patient's symptoms are consistent with a pituitary adenoma, which is most likely caused by abnormal growth of the adenohypophysis. Adenomas of the pituitary gland are usually due to proliferation of lactotroph cells, leading to hyperprolactinemia and suppression of gonadotropins causing secondary amenorrhea. Bitemporal hemianopsia and headaches may also develop due to compression of the optic chiasm as the adenoma grows. While a large non secreting pituitary adenoma could also explain her symptoms, the absence of other hypopituitarism symptoms makes prolactinoma more likely. Incorrect Options: Option A - Astrocytes: Astrocytomas are associated with rapidly progressive symptoms and typically occur in older individuals moreover this patient's symptoms, including secondary amenorrhea and bitemporal hemianopsia, are more indicative of a pituitary adenoma, which is caused by abnormal growth of cells in the adenohypophysis, not astrocytes. Option C - Arachnoid cap cells: Arachnoid cap cells are not related to the symptoms described in the question stem, which suggest abnormal growth affecting the menstrual cycle and vision. questions.stem: A 32-year-old male with a smoking history presents with cough, dyspnea, and hemoptysis. On examination, he has bilateral crackles in his lungs and decreased urine output. A chest X-ray shows diffuse pulmonary infiltrates, and urinalysis reveals microscopic hematuria. A renal biopsy is performed, and the pathology report shows linear IgG and C3 deposition along the basement membrane. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A 32-year-old male with a smoking history presents with cough, dyspnea, and hemoptysis. On examination, he has bilateral crackles in his lungs and decreased urine output. A chest X-ray shows diffuse pulmonary infiltrates, and urinalysis reveals microscopic hematuria. A renal biopsy is performed, and the pathology report shows linear IgG and C3 deposition along the basement membrane. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: Correct Option B- Goodpasture syndrome: This patient's clinical presentation, with hemoptysis, diffuse pulmonary infiltrates, and renal involvement, raises suspicion of an autoimmune disease affecting both organs. Goodpasture syndrome is a rare autoimmune disease characterized by the presence of autoantibodies against type IV collagen, a component of the glomerular and alveolar basement membrane. The most common presentation is acute kidney injury with pulmonary hemorrhage. The diagnosis is made by demonstrating the presence of anti-GBM antibodies or by showing linear IgG and C3 deposition along the basement membrane on renal biopsy. In this patient, the renal biopsy showed linear IgG and C3 deposition along the basement membrane, confirming the diagnosis of Goodpasture syndrome. The presence of pulmonary hemorrhage on imaging and hemoptysis further supports this diagnosis. Incorrect Options: Option A- Wegener's granulomatosis: Option A (Wegener's granulomatosis) is an autoimmune disease that affects small blood vessels and can involve the kidneys, lungs, and upper respiratory tract. While the clinical presentation of hemoptysis and pulmonary infiltrates may be similar to Goodpasture syndrome, the histopathology findings are different. In Wegener's granulomatosis, the characteristic histopathological feature is necrotizing granulomatous inflammation, not linear IgG and C3 deposition along the basement membrane. Therefore, option A is an incorrect answer in this scenario. Option C- Sarcoidosis: Option C (Sarcoidosis) is a multisystem inflammatory disease affecting the lungs, skin, eyes, and other organs. The hallmark histopathological feature of sarcoidosis is non-caseating granulomas, not linear IgG and C3 deposition along the basement membrane. While sarcoidosis can present with pulmonary infiltrates and renal involvement, the presence of linear IgG and C3 deposition on renal biopsy is not consistent with this diagnosis. Therefore, option C is an incorrect answer in this scenario. Option D- Alport syndrome: Option D (Alport syndrome) is a genetic disorder that affects the glomerular basement membrane and can cause kidney disease and hearing loss. While it can present with hematuria, the presence of pulmonary infiltrates, hemoptysis, and linear IgG and C3 deposition on renal biopsy is not consistent with this diagnosis. Therefore, option D is an incorrect answer in this scenario. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 36-year-old male presents to the clinic with a complaint of severe shortness of breath. The patient never smoked and is also seeking treatment with a hepatologist for liver issues. On examination, a prolonged wheeze is appreciated. Spirometry is performed and forced expiratory volume in the first second after the bronchodilator is 65% of the predictive value. A clinical diagnosis of emphysema is made. The patient inquires about the cause of the disease at this young age. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
questions.stemHtml: A 36-year-old male presents to the clinic with a complaint of severe shortness of breath. The patient never smoked and is also seeking treatment with a hepatologist for liver issues. On examination, a prolonged wheeze is appreciated. Spirometry is performed and forced expiratory volume in the first second after the bronchodilator is 65% of the predictive value. A clinical diagnosis of emphysema is made. The patient inquires about the cause of the disease at this young age. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency Alpha-1 antitrypsin is a protease inhibitor which is synthesised by the liver. It inactivates the neutrophil elastase and protects the lung tissue. It is caused by a genetic mutation which causes a conformational change in the structure of alpha-1 antitrypsin. The dysfunctional protein affects the liver by accumulating in the hepatocytes' endoplasmic reticulum resulting in hepatitis and liver cirrhosis. In the lungs, its deficiency results in an uninhibited activity of neutrophil elastase, which causes pulmonary parenchyma destruction and results in pan acinar emphysema. Patients are < 60 years of age. Incorrect Options: Option B - Smoking Nicotine and smoking cause the inactivation of protease inhibitors and form reactive oxygen species. Smoking results in the destruction of respiratory bronchioles, resulting in centrilobular emphysema. Option C - Bullae formation In giant bullous emphysema, large bullae are formed, which cause the destruction of surrounding pulmonary tissue. Option D - Scar formation The chronic inflammation results in scar formation due to quartz exposure which results in cicatricial emphysema. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 44-year-old female with suspected myasthenia gravis is planned for robotic thymectomy under general anesthesia. During the preoperative anesthesia evaluation, he related a history of recurrent pulmonary aspiration and significant ocular weakness. Which of the following antibodies are likely to be present in the plasma and can be used for preoperative screening of myasthenia gravis?
questions.stemHtml: A 44-year-old female with suspected myasthenia gravis is planned for robotic thymectomy under general anesthesia. During the preoperative anesthesia evaluation, he related a history of recurrent pulmonary aspiration and significant ocular weakness. Which of the following antibodies are likely to be present in the plasma and can be used for preoperative screening of myasthenia gravis?
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Anti-muscle-specific kinase antibodies: Postsynaptic acetylcholine receptor antibodies are the most common antibodies found in patients with myasthenia gravis. These antibodies are present in nearly 95% of patients diagnosed with myasthenia gravis. Other groups of patients with significantly higher involvement of bulbar muscles have muscle-specific kinase antibodies. These antibodies occur in nearly 50% of patients with myasthenia gravis. They are produced against the phosphorylating enzyme in the skeletal muscles. Their role is defined in patients with bulbar involvement or in patients seronegative for anti-acetylcholine receptor antibodies. The sensitivity is in the following order: acetylcholine receptor (postsynaptic) > muscle-specific kinase antibodies. Incorrect Options: Option A - Anti-acetylcholine receptor antibodies (pre-synaptic): Unlike Lambert-Eaton syndrome where the antibodies are against presynaptic calcium channels, myasthenia is primarily a postsynaptic disorder. Antibodies are produced against postsynaptic receptors or muscle-specific kinase. This describes the presynaptic antibody, which is not related to myasthenia. Option B - Anti-acetylcholinesterase antibodies: Acetylcholinesterase is an enzyme that metabolizes the acetylcholine released in the synaptic cleft. Destruction of this enzyme would produce symptoms similar to organophosphate poisoning. This would lead to increased activity of both muscarinic and nicotinic receptors. Myasthenia is primarily a disease of nicotinic receptors, and these antibodies have no relation to myasthenia gravis. Option D - Anti-thymocyte globulin antibodies: Patients with thymoma have a high incidence of myasthenia gravis. This has been attributed to a T-cell-mediated autoimmune response observed in patients with hyperactive thymus. This, however, is not related to anti-thymocyte globulin antibodies. These antibodies are therapeutically used in patients who receive transplanted organs and are used for immunosuppression. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option A- MRI: MRI scans are the best imaging modalities for diagnosing coarctation of the aorta. Through MRI, detailed images of the aorta are obtained using radio waves and magnetic fields. MRI provides information about the exact location, size, and severity of the aortic narrowing, damage to surrounding blood vessels and other etiologies of the heart. Treatment is based on the results of the MRI. Incorrect Options: Option B- ECG: ECG can show the hypertrophy of the ventricular walls, which can be confirmed by echocardiography. ECG is not the investigation of choice as ECG does not provide information about the underlying cause (coarctation of the aorta) of the hypertrophy Option C- Chest X-ray: X-ray chest is often normal in early childhood patients with coarctation of the aorta. Later in life, the indentation of the descending aorta (3 signs) and notching of the ribs due to collaterals can be seen on chest X-rays. Option D- FAST: Focused abdominal sonography for trauma is not the investigation of choice in patients with coarctation of the aorta. FAST is done in patients to assess for hemopericardium and hemoperitoneum in trauma patients. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 75-year-old patient is admitted to the hospital for respiratory distress and is treated for influenza. After 5 days of treatment, he continues to have a fever. On day 8, the nurse inquires about removing droplet precautions. What is the most appropriate course of action?
questions.stemHtml: A 75-year-old patient is admitted to the hospital for respiratory distress and is treated for influenza. After 5 days of treatment, he continues to have a fever. On day 8, the nurse inquires about removing droplet precautions. What is the most appropriate course of action?

options.label: A
options.text: Continue droplet precautions until the fever is resolved

options.label: B
options.text: Discontinue droplet precautions since the patient finished treatment

options.label: C
options.text: Relocate the patient to a negative-pressure room

questions.answerText: Continue droplet precautions until the fever is resolved
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Continue droplet precautions until the fever is resolved Influenza is predominantly transmitted via droplets. The virus is shed from the airway and spread by coughing and sneezing. Other ways of transmission are of lesser importance. Shedding of the virus may continue despite treatment. The current recommendation indicates that droplet precautions can be dropped after 7 days from the onset of the illness or 24 hours after resolution of the symptoms (whichever is longer). In this particular example, the patient experienced a fever, so isolation precaution should be continued. Incorrect Options: Option B - Discontinue droplet precautions since the patient finished treatment: This option is incorrect because the patient still has a fever after 5 days of influenza treatment. Even though the patient completed the treatment course, the persistence of the fever suggests that the infection may not have completely resolved. Droplet precautions should be continued until the fever has resolved to prevent the potential spread of the infection to others. Option C - Relocate the patient to a negative-pressure room: This option is also incorrect. Negative-pressure rooms are typically used for patients with airborne infections, such as tuberculosis or measles, where the infectious particles can remain suspended in the air for an extended period. Influenza is primarily transmitted through respiratory droplets, not through the airborne route. Thus, relocating the patient to a negative-pressure room is not necessary in this case. Option D - Repeat treatment with Tamiflu: This option is incorrect because it assumes that the patient's fever is persisting due to an inadequate response to the initial Tamiflu treatment. However, it's important to note that some patients with influenza, especially elderly individuals or those with compromised immune systems, may experience a prolonged fever even after appropriate antiviral treatment. Repeating Tamiflu without any clinical indication may not be necessary and could lead to potential side effects without any significant benefit. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A first-time mother presents with her 9-day-old infant who has experienced seizures. The infant had an uncomplicated term delivery and has been otherwise well. The infant has been and remains afebrile. The mother reports diluting the baby's formula. What is the most likely cause of this infant's seizures?
questions.stemHtml: A first-time mother presents with her 9-day-old infant who has experienced seizures. The infant had an uncomplicated term delivery and has been otherwise well. The infant has been and remains afebrile. The mother reports diluting the baby's formula. What is the most likely cause of this infant's seizures?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Hyponatremia: In a well newborn without a fever, hyponatremia is the most common cause of seizures. Water intoxication is the most common cause of hyponatremia during infancy. Infants are unable to concentrate urine adequately, so parents who dilute formula or give their infants tap water put their infants at risk. Other causes of neonatal seizures also include neonatal encephalopathy and hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy, structural brain injuries, including ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke; glucose or other electrolyte abnormalities; and systemic or CNS infections. In a well-baby, a genetic epilepsy syndrome such as benign familial neonatal epilepsy may be the cause. Incorrect Options: Option A - Hypokalemia: Hypokalemia is uncommon in infancy and does not typically cause seizures. Option C - Hypocalcemia: Hypocalcemia is also a common cause of seizures in neonates, so serum calcium levels should be checked. In fact, all infants have a slight decline in serum calcium levels with a nadir at 24 to 48 hours. Symptomatic hypocalcemia is more common in infants of diabetic mothers, preterm infants, or infants with a history of anoxic encephalopathy. Option D - Hypomagnesemia: Hypomagnesemia is not as common as hypocalcemia, but symptoms of hypomagnesemia mimic those of hypocalcemia. It is difficult to correct hypocalcemia if the serum magnesium is also low. Therefore, infants with seizures should have a comprehensive evaluation of their electrolytes. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option B - Oral valganciclovir: Antiviral treatment is indicated for infants with symptomatic congenital CMV infection (generally defined as involvement of at least one end-organ symptom). questions.answerText: Combined low dose aspirin and low molecular heparin
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Combined low dose aspirin and low molecular heparin: This lady meets the diagnostic criteria for antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) by virtue of an episode of pregnancy loss beyond ten weeks and a persistently positive lupus anticoagulant. Incorrect Options: Option B - Low dose aspirin: A combined dose of aspirin and low molecular heparin is recommended Option C - Low molecular weight heparin: A combined dose of aspirin and low molecular heparin is recommended Option D - Unfractionated heparin: A combined dose of aspirin and low molecular heparin is recommended @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 72-year-old male is admitted to the ICU for aspergillosis. Liposomal amphotericin B is ordered. Shortly after the infusion, the patient develops chills, a fever, and diffuse muscle pain. His vital signs are stable, and the infusion is continued. A day later, the patient experiences anuria. What is the most plausible reason for his anuria?
questions.stemHtml: A 72-year-old male is admitted to the ICU for aspergillosis. Liposomal amphotericin B is ordered. Shortly after the infusion, the patient develops chills, a fever, and diffuse muscle pain. His vital signs are stable, and the infusion is continued. A day later, the patient experiences anuria. What is the most plausible reason for his anuria?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Renal ischemia: Amphotericin is a highly nephrotoxic medication. The mechanism of toxicity is related to enhanced renal tubuloglomerular feedback, leading to vasoconstriction of the renal arteriole and ischemia. This causes irreversible renal ischemia and subsequent renal failure. A liposomal modification of amphotericin B has a slightly lower nephrotoxic profile than the original drug formulation. Liposomal amphotericin is also preferred to treat central nervous infections due to a slightly better penetration. Incorrect Options: Option B - Rhabdomyolysis: Rhabdomyolysis is a condition where damaged skeletal muscle tissue releases its contents, including myoglobin, into the bloodstream. Myoglobin is harmful to the kidneys and can cause acute kidney injury (AKI) when large amounts are filtered by the kidneys. While rhabdomyolysis can cause diffuse muscle pain, it is not the most plausible reason for anuria in this case. The patient's symptoms of chills, fever, and diffuse muscle pain are more likely related to the infusion of liposomal amphotericin B, which is known to cause these side effects. Option C - Dehydration: Dehydration can certainly lead to acute kidney injury (AKI), and it is important to consider fluid status in any patient with kidney dysfunction. However, in this case, the patient was just admitted, and there is no indication that he has a history of prior low fluid intake or dehydration. The most likely cause of anuria in this patient is the nephrotoxic effect of liposomal amphotericin B, leading to renal ischemia. Option D - Tubular obstruction: Tubular obstruction can occur in patients receiving certain medications, such as acyclovir, leading to acute kidney injury. However, this patient is receiving liposomal amphotericin B, not acyclovir. While amphotericin B can also cause kidney damage, it does so through renal ischemia, not tubular obstruction. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 20-year-old female college student presents to her primary care physician complaining of fatigue, dizziness, and difficulty concentrating. She has had intermittent diarrhoea for the past several months. She also reports a rash on her face and hands that worsens with sun exposure. On examination, the patient is found to have a rash on her face and upper extremities as shown in the image below. Complete blood count is normal. Urinalysis reveals elevated levels of neutral amino acids. What is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 20-year-old female college student presents to her primary care physician complaining of fatigue, dizziness, and difficulty concentrating. She has had intermittent diarrhoea for the past several months. She also reports a rash on her face and hands that worsens with sun exposure. On examination, the patient is found to have a rash on her face and upper extremities as shown in the image below. Complete blood count is normal. Urinalysis reveals elevated levels of neutral amino acids. What is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Hartnup disease: Hartnup disease is an autosomal recessive disorder that is caused by a defective neutral amino acid transporter involved in the transport of neutral amino acids across the intestinal and renal epithelial cells. The neutral amino acids include tryptophan (a precursor of niacin), valine and phenylalanine etc. This results in tryptophan deficiency, which leads to a range of symptoms similar to pellagra, including diarrhoea, dermatitis (photosensitive skin rash), and neurologic symptoms such as psychosis and cerebellar ataxia. The skin rash in Hartnup disease typically occurs on the face and upper extremities and is exacerbated by sunlight exposure. The rash can be erythematous, papular, or scaly. The diagnosis of Hartnup disease is typically made based on clinical presentation and laboratory findings. Laboratory studies may show increased excretion of neutral amino acids in the urine. Treatment of Hartnup disease involves managing symptoms and preventing exacerbations. This can include avoiding sunlight exposure, supplementing with tryptophan or other neutral amino acids, and providing supportive care for neurological and gastrointestinal symptoms. Incorrect Options: Option A - Celiac disease: Celiac disease is an autoimmune disorder characterized by gluten insensitivity that can cause gastrointestinal symptoms such as diarrhoea, as well as anemia, osteoporosis, and a skin rash (dermatitis herpetiformis). However, the rash in celiac disease is symmetrically distributed over extensor surfaces and it is not associated with elevated levels of neutral amino acids in the urine. Option C - Systemic lupus erythematous: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is an autoimmune disorder characterized by multi-system involvement, including the skin, joints, and kidneys. While it can cause skin rash, this patient doesn’t have other characteristic features of SLE like arthralgias, pancytopenia etc. Also, SLE has no effect on urinary neutral amino acid levels. Option D - Porphyria cutanea tarda: Porphyria cutanea tarda is a disorder of heme metabolism that can cause skin blistering and fragility. While the patient does have a skin rash, her gastrointestinal and neurologic symptoms as well as elevated urinary neutral amino acid levels make Hartnup disease a more likely diagnosis. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Which of the following is a systemic side effect after prolonged use of ipratropium?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following is a systemic side effect after prolonged use of ipratropium?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Urinary retention Up to 20% of ipratropium can be absorbed given as MDI can be absorbed via mucosal membranes of the mouth or systemic absorption through the pulmonary circulation. Consequently, some systemic side effect can be possible. Anticholinergic agents are known to cause urinary retention. In pooled analyzed of 19 randomized trial symptoms of urinary retention was more frequently present in a patient taking inhaled anticholinergic that control group. On the other hand UPLIFT trial showed no-statistically significant increase in the rate of urinary retention. Finally, in small trial 25 patient with BPH, no exacerbation of symptoms was noted. Consequently, the patient should be counseled that urinary retention might occur, but it is not universal complication. Incorrect Options: Options B - Immunosuppression: This is not a typical side effect of anticholinergic medications such as ipratropium. Immunosuppression is more commonly seen with long-term use of corticosteroids, which can suppress the body's immune response. Options C - Dry mouth: While it is true that anticholinergic medications can cause dry mouth, this is typically a local side effect due to the medication acting on the muscarinic receptors in the salivary glands to reduce saliva production. However, in the case of inhaled ipratropium, the medication is mainly acting on the receptors in the lungs and not the salivary glands. Therefore, while dry mouth can occur, it is less common and generally not considered a systemic side effect. Option D - Hair loss: Hair loss is not a known side effect of anticholinergic medications like ipratropium. Hair loss can occur due to various reasons, including genetics, certain diseases, stress, and the use of certain medications, but ipratropium is not known to cause this. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option A - The ascending reticular activating system: The ascending reticular activating system (ARAS) is a network of neurons originating in the tegmentum of the upper pons and midbrain, which are important in the maintenance of alertness (option a correct). This group of neurons contains two branches, one that projects through the thalamus and another that projects through the hypothalamus and basal forebrain and from those structures to the cerebral cortex. questions.solution: Correct Option A- Chordae tendineae: The chordae tendineae are cord-like tendons that attach to the papillary muscles and the edges of the mitral and tricuspid valves in the heart. They play a crucial role in preventing the prolapse of the mitral valve into the left atrium during systole. In mitral valve prolapse (MVP), the chordae tendineae may be elongated or ruptured , leading to the abnormal bulging of the mitral valve into the left atrium. This can result in mitral regurgitation, which can lead to symptoms such as shortness of breath and palpitations, as seen in this patient. Incorrect Options: Option B- Papillary muscles: The papillary muscles are small, cone-shaped muscles that are attached to the chordae tendineae and the ventricular walls. They contract during systole , pulling the chordae tendineae taut and preventing the prolapse of the mitral valve into the left atrium. However, in MVP, the papillary muscles are usually normal and the defect lies in the chordae tendineae. Option C- Tricuspid valve: The tricuspid valve is located between the right atrium and right ventricle , and is not involved in mitral valve prolapse. Option D- Aortic valve: The aortic valve is located between the left ventricle and the aorta , and is not involved in mitral valve prolapse. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option A - Asbestos exposure increases the risk of lung cancer associated with cigarette smoke exposure: The risk of lung cancer associated with exposure to both asbestos and cigarette smoke appears to be multiplicative. Incorrect Options: Option B - Coughing, sputum production, and wheezing are the most common presenting symptoms: Coughing, sputum production, and wheezing are not the most common presenting symptoms of asbestos-induced lung disease. The most common presenting symptom of asbestos-induced lung disease is dyspnea, which can be a result of interstitial lung disease (asbestosis) or lung cancer. Asbestos exposure primarily affects the lungs' interstitium, leading to fibrosis and scarring, which can cause progressive dyspnea. Option C - Antinuclear antibody, rheumatoid factor, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate have prognostic implications : Antinuclear antibody (ANA), rheumatoid factor (RF), and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) are not specific markers for asbestos-induced lung disease. These are nonspecific laboratory tests and are not used for diagnosing or prognosticating asbestos-related lung conditions. Asbestosis and asbestos-related lung diseases are diagnosed based on clinical history, occupational exposure, radiographic findings, and pulmonary function tests. Option D - Cigarette exposure does not increase the risk of lung cancer associated with asbestos exposure : Cigarette exposure does increase the risk of lung cancer associated with asbestos exposure. questions.stem: A 17-year-old male presents to the clinic with delayed puberty and small testes. He is diagnosed with Klinefelter syndrome. What is the recommended treatment for this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 17-year-old male presents to the clinic with delayed puberty and small testes. He is diagnosed with Klinefelter syndrome. What is the recommended treatment for this patient?
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Testosterone replacement therapy: The treatment of Klinefelter syndrome is primarily aimed at managing the symptoms and associated health issues. Testosterone replacement therapy (TRT ) is the mainstay of treatment for hypogonadism in males with Klinefelter syndrome. TRT helps to increase muscle mass and strength, reduce body fat, improve bone density, and increase libido. TRT can be administered through injections, patches, gels, or pellets. In addition to TRT, other therapies may be recommended based on specific symptoms and health issues. For example, speech therapy may be recommended for individuals with speech and language delays, while physical therapy may be recommended to improve muscle strength and coordination. Psychosocial support may also be helpful to manage social and emotional challenges associated with Klinefelter syndrome. In some cases, fertility treatment may be an option for individuals with Klinefelter syndrome who wish to father children. Options for fertility treatment may include assisted reproductive technologies such as intrauterine insemination (IUI) or in vitro fertilisation (IVF) with intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI) using donor sperm or sperm retrieved from the individual's testes. Incorrect Options: Option A - Human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG): Human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) is a hormone used to stimulate the testes to produce testosterone and sperm. However, hCG is not a recommended treatment for Klinefelter syndrome. This is because boys with Klinefelter syndrome have an extra X chromosome, which leads to abnormal testicular development and low testosterone levels. While hCG may stimulate the testes to produce testosterone, it is unlikely to be effective in treating the underlying hormonal imbalance in Klinefelter syndrome . Option B - Clomiphene citrate: Clomiphene citrate is a medication that is sometimes used to treat infertility in men with low levels of luteinising hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH). However, it is not a recommended treatment for Klinefelter syndrome. Boys with Klinefelter syndrome have normal or high levels of LH and FSH, but they do not produce enough testosterone due to abnormal testicular development. Clomiphene citrate would not be effective in treating this underlying hormonal imbalance. Option D - Oestrogen replacement therapy: Oestrogen replacement therapy is not a recommended treatment for Klinefelter syndrome. In fact, it may exacerbate the symptoms associated with the disorder, such as gynecomastia (breast enlargement). Boys with Klinefelter syndrome have an extra X chromosome, which can lead to an increase in oestrogen levels. Oestrogen replacement therapy would not be appropriate for these patients, as it may further increase their oestrogen levels and exacerbate their symptoms. @Neet_pg_bot

Pulmonary function test shows no difference in FEV1 before and after inhaled short-term bronchodilator. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.label: A
options.text: Introduce steroids to sensitize airway to sympathomimetics

options.label: B
options.text: Avoid prescribing sympathomimetics due to lack of airway responsiveness

options.label: C

options.label: D
options.text: Prescribe a short acting bronchodilator for use as needed

questions.answerText: Prescribe a short acting bronchodilator for use as needed
questions.solution: Correct Option D - Prescribe a short acting bronchodilator for use as needed: Short-acting bronchodilators provide the best relief of symptoms in COPD and should be prescribed for all patients with minimal symptoms and low risk of exacerbation. Incorrect Options: Option A - Introduce steroids to sensitize airway to sympathomimetics: This option is not appropriate as it suggests the use of steroids to sensitize the airways to sympathomimetics. In this patient with minimally symptomatic COPD and no evidence of bronchodilator responsiveness on pulmonary function testing, starting steroids is not indicated. Option B - Avoid prescribing sympathomimetics due to lack of airway responsiveness: This option is also not appropriate as it suggests avoiding sympathomimetics based on the lack of airway responsiveness on pulmonary function testing. Short-acting bronchodilators (sympathomimetics) are the mainstay of treatment for relieving symptoms in COPD, regardless of the degree of airway responsiveness on testing. Many patients with COPD experience symptom relief and improved exercise capacity with short-acting bronchodilators, even if their FEV1 does not show significant improvement. Option C - Repeat the test after three months: Repeating the pulmonary function test after only three months is not necessary or indicated in this case. Pulmonary function testing is typically performed annually to monitor disease progression and response to treatment.
