questions.stem: A 17-year-old girl is taken to the doctor because she has never had her menstrual period. She is in the fifteenth percentile for weight and the forty-fifth percentile for height. The vital signs are within regular ranges. Facial hair, clitoromegaly, and coarse, curly pubic hair extending to both thighs' inner area are all visible on examination. She does not have mammary breast tissue. Ultrasound reveals inguinal testes but no uterus or ovaries. Which of the following is the most probable underlying cause of these symptoms in this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 17-year-old girl is taken to the doctor because she has never had her menstrual period. She is in the fifteenth percentile for weight and the forty-fifth percentile for height. The vital signs are within regular ranges. Facial hair, clitoromegaly, and coarse, curly pubic hair extending to both thighs' inner area are all visible on examination. She does not have mammary breast tissue. Ultrasound reveals inguinal testes but no uterus or ovaries. Which of the following is the most probable underlying cause of these symptoms in this patient?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - 5-alpha reductase deficiency: The patient presents with the clinical features and investigative findings of 5-alpha reductase deficiency. Due to the very low testosterone levels produced by the fetal testes, 5- reductase deficiency results in lower levels of dihydrotestosterone (DHT), which is needed for the masculinisation of external genitalia. Affected individuals have external genitalia ranging from female to microphallus with hypospadias at birth. Increased testosterone production during adolescence by completely developed intra-abdominal or inguinal testes, on the other hand, results in masculinisation of the genitalia and the development of male secondary sexual characteristics such as body hair (which can be mistaken for hirsutism). Menarche does not occur because the uterus, ovaries, and glandular breast tissue are missing, and the patient is karyotypically male (XY). Genetic testing confirms the diagnosis, which should show a mutation in the SRD5A2 gene on chromosome 2p. Because of the effects of testosterone on the brain, patients with a 5-alpha reductase deficiency may acquire a male gender identity. Such individuals are treated with testosterone supplementation, phalloplasty, and orchidopexy. Following the conclusion of longitudinal growth, patients with a female gender identity should undergo gonadectomy followed by oestrogen substitution therapy due to environmental and psychosocial factors. Incorrect Options: Option B - Mullerian duct agenesis: Mullerian duct agenesis presents with primary amenorrhoea. On ultrasound, isolated agenesis of the Mullerian ducts would show an absent uterus. Clitoromegaly, hirsutism, and impaired breast development are not anticipated in Mullerian agenesis. Instead, owing to vaginal atresia, patients have a blind vaginal pouch. Option C - Aromatase deficiency: Aromatase deficiency in a female-phenotype infant can cause primary amenorrhea, clitoromegaly/micropenis, impaired breast development, and hirsutism at puberty. However, imaging would reveal a uterus and ovaries because the patients are karyotypically female. Patients with this condition are usually tall. Option D - Complete androgen insensitivity: Complete androgen insensitivity syndrome patients are genetically male but phenotypically feminine. Because they lack a uterus or ovaries, they present with primary amenorrhea, and ultrasound would reveal intra-abdominal or inguinal testes, which could cause pain as they develop during puberty. On the other hand, patients with androgen insensitivity syndrome grow normally, with no clitoromegaly or pronounced body hair. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 44-year-old man came to the clinic with complaints of dysuria, urinary frequency, and urgency for the last 3 days. He has had hypertension and diabetes mellitus for the last eight years. Urine culture reveals Proteus mirabilis and has been adequately treated. He has had recurrent episodes of urinary tract infections in the last two years. This patient is most likely to develop which of the following conditions?
questions.stemHtml: A 44-year-old man came to the clinic with complaints of dysuria, urinary frequency, and urgency for the last 3 days. He has had hypertension and diabetes mellitus for the last eight years. Urine culture reveals Proteus mirabilis and has been adequately treated. He has had recurrent episodes of urinary tract infections in the last two years. This patient is most likely to develop which of the following conditions?
questions.solution: Correct Option C: Struvite stones. Struvite stones (magnesium ammonium phosphate) are formed due to upper urinary tract infections from urease-positive organisms, i.e. Proteus mirabilis, Klebsiella pneumonia, Enterobacter, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Urease produced by these organisms converts urea into ammonia. Increased alkalinization of the urine due to raised ammonia levels leads to the precipitation of ammonium magnesium phosphate salt resulting in stone formation. These stones are large and are usually present in the renal pelvis and calyces. "Staghorn" refers to a branched kidney stone occupying the renal pelvis and at least one calyceal system. Struvite stones usually present with urinary tract infections or hematuria, not as acute renal pain. The mainstay of the treatment is treating the underlying infection, hydration, acidification of urine and ultimately, surgical removal of the stone like PCNL and ESWL. Incorrect options: Option A: Cystine stones These stones are moderately radio-opaque and are formed due to impaired proximal renal tubular absorption of dibasic amino acids which are cystine, ornithine, lysine and arginine, not due to infections, and are formed in acidified urine. Usually begins in childhood. Can form staghorn calculi. Sodium cyanide nitroprusside test ⊕. Treatment: low sodium diet, alkalinization of urine, chelating agents (eg, tiopronin, penicillamine) if refractory. Option B: Calcium oxalate stones Calcium stones most common (80%); calcium oxalate more common than calcium phosphate stones. Can result from ethylene glycol (antifreeze) ingestion, vitamin C overuse, hypocitraturia (usually associated with decreased urine pH), malabsorption (eg, Crohn disease). Option D: Uric acid stones These stones are most common type of radiolucent renal stone and are formed due to increased uric acid levels in the blood and urine, either due to increased intake or to the production of uric acid inside the body. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Which of the following symptoms is inconsistent with a diagnosis of Guillain-Barre syndrome?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following symptoms is inconsistent with a diagnosis of Guillain-Barre syndrome?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Persistent asymmetry of weakness: Acute inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy (AIDP), or “Guillain-Barre syndrome,” is an autoimmune, areflexic, ascending weakness with mild sensory changes that progresses over a few weeks. It is classically a demyelinating process, although axonal damage may occur in cases of severe demyelination. Predominantly axonal variants also exist (e.g. Miller-Fisher syndrome, acute motor axonal neuropathy). It is often associated with a preceding respiratory infection, gastrointestinal infection, surgery, or vaccination. Characteristic manifestations include: Progressive upper and lower extremity weakness, which may also involve facial, oropharyngeal, and respiratory muscles Areflexia or hyporeflexia Progression over days to weeks (by definition, progression ends by 4 weeks after onset) Symmetry of weakness Mild sensory changes Interscapular or low back pain Cranial nerve palsies (45-75% of cases), often bilateral and involving facial nerves Dysautonomia (e.g. orthostasis, anhidrosis, urinary retention, arrhythmias), occurring in approximately 66% of patients Lack of fever Elevated CSF protein levels persisting beyond the first week of symptoms, in the absence of pleocytosis (”albuminocytological dissociation”) Nerve conduction slowing or blockage on nerve conduction studies Recovery over weeks Findings that are inconsistent with a diagnosis of Guillain-Barre syndrome include: Persistently asymmetric weakness Clear sensory level Severe bowel or bladder dysfunction at the onset of symptoms A marked CSF pleocytosis should also raise suspicion for an alternative diagnosis. Incorrect Options: Option A - Sensory Involvement: Guillain-Barre syndrome (GBS) is primarily a motor neuropathy and does not typically involve significant sensory changes. While mild sensory changes may occur in some cases, they are not a prominent feature of GBS. Patients with GBS may experience tingling or mild sensory symptoms, but the hallmark of the condition is progressive weakness rather than sensory deficits. Option C - Cranial Nerve Palsies: Cranial nerve palsies are actually consistent with a diagnosis of Guillain-Barre syndrome. Approximately 45-75% of GBS cases may involve cranial nerves, often resulting in bilateral facial nerve palsies. Other cranial nerves can also be affected, leading to a variety of cranial nerve-related symptoms such as difficulty swallowing, double vision, or facial weakness. Option D - Dysautonomia: Dysautonomia, which refers to dysfunction of the autonomic nervous system, is a common feature of Guillain-Barre syndrome. About 66% of patients with GBS experience dysautonomia, which may present as symptoms like orthostatic hypotension, changes in heart rate, abnormal sweating patterns, and urinary retention. Dysautonomia is consistent with the demyelinating process affecting the autonomic nerves in GBS. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 75-year-old male with Lewy body dementia develops aspiration pneumonia in the nursing home. The patient’s condition is not addressed in a timely manner, and the pneumonia progresses into a parapneumonic effusion with the eventual development of an empyema. Empyemas characteristically consist of anaerobic organisms which are polymicrobial in nature. Which of the following is the most common group/species of organisms found in these infections?
questions.stemHtml: A 75-year-old male with Lewy body dementia develops aspiration pneumonia in the nursing home. Empyemas characteristically consist of anaerobic organisms which are polymicrobial in nature. Which of the following is the most common group/species of organisms found in these infections?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Fusobacterium nucleatum: The most common anaerobic species in pulmonary empyemas was found to be Fusobacterium nucleatum, which are small spindle shaped organisms frequently present in gum disease and contributes to dental plaque formation. The organism is known for its characteristic to adhere to both type IV collagen and other microorganisms, and is the most likely oral bacterium to be involved in infections in distant sites of the body. Incorrect Options: Option A - Microaerophilic streptococci: Though slightly less common than fusobacterium, is a frequent pathogen involved in parapneumonic effusions and empyemas and more often than not is a component of a polymicrobial infection with anaerobes and aerobes. Option C - Prevotella: Is a non-motile, anaerobic, gram negative rod which is part of the normal flora of the mouth and is involved in gingival disease. The species has the propensity to cause infections at distant sites of the body, especially the lungs through aspiration. Option D - Bacteroides species: Are anaerobic gram negative rods, and are a component of the normal flora of the gut. They have the potential to cause abscesses throughout the body. The most common species encountered in the laboratory is B. fragilis, which are susceptible to carbapenems and metronidazole yet have a high rate of resistance to penicillin, cefoxitin, clindamycin, and fluoroquinolones. @Neet_pg_bot

She also complains of early satiety. On upper endoscopy, her duodenum is narrowed, but no mucosal lesions are identified. Abdominal CT is suggestive of annular pancreas. Which of the following is indicated for the definitive management of this condition?
questions.stemHtml: A 30-year-old female patient is evaluated for projectile vomiting and epigastric pain that has been recurrent over 3 years but has increased in severity over the past 6 months. She also complains of early satiety. On upper endoscopy, her duodenum is narrowed, but no mucosal lesions are identified. Abdominal CT is suggestive of annular pancreas. Which of the following is indicated for the definitive management of this condition?

options.label: B
options.text: Surgical resection of the annular ring

options.label: D
options.text: Surgical bypass of the annular ring

questions.answerText: Surgical bypass of the annular ring
questions.solution: Correct Option D - Surgical bypass of the annular ring: Annular pancreas is a congenital abnormality of the pancreas defined by a ring of pancreatic tissue encapsulating the descending portion of the duodenum, most likely due to incomplete rotation of the embryologic ventral pancreatic bud. Since it is usually asymptomatic, the incidence is unknown, but it appears to occur rarely. It is characterized as complete or incomplete and classified into subtypes based upon the drainage of the annular duct. Symptoms may occur as early as the neonatal period, but age of onset is determined by severity of obstruction. Typically, adults present between the ages of 20 and 50 with chronic abdominal pain, early satiety, nausea, and vomiting. Performance of cholangiopancreatogram allows delineation of the structure of the annular duct and accessory pancreatic duct. In patients who are symptomatic, treatment is surgery to relieve gastric outlet or duodenal obstruction by a bypass of the annulus. Incorrect Options: Option A - Pancreaticoduodenectomy: Pancreaticoduodenectomy or Whipple procedure may be indicated in patients with obstructive pancreatic duct stones and chronic pancreatitis or in those who have a potentially malignant periampullary lesion. Option B - Surgical resection of the annular ring: Surgical resection is associated with pancreatitis and fistula formation, without complete relief of the obstruction. Option C - Biliary stent: Biliary stenting is not indicated for the management of annular pancreas in the absence of obstructive jaundice @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 60-year-old male recently diagnosed with AML (M4 variant) is on standard induction therapy with cytarabine (seven day continuous infusion) + an anthracycline (given days 1-3) (7+3 therapy). The patient is paraplegic and is very concerned about developing diarrhea and mucositis during induction therapy. Which of the following medications has been demonstrated to reduce the incidence of severe diarrhea in patients undergoing induction therapy for AML?
questions.stemHtml: A 60-year-old male recently diagnosed with AML (M4 variant) is on standard induction therapy with cytarabine (seven day continuous infusion) + an anthracycline (given days 1-3) (7+3 therapy). The patient is paraplegic and is very concerned about developing diarrhea and mucositis during induction therapy. Which of the following medications has been demonstrated to reduce the incidence of severe diarrhea in patients undergoing induction therapy for AML?
questions.solution: Correct Option D- Palifermin: Palifermin is a medication that belongs to the class of keratinocyte growth factors. It plays a crucial role in promoting the growth and repair of epithelial tissues, including the gastrointestinal (GI) mucosa. Patients undergoing intensive chemotherapy regimens, such as those used in acute myeloid leukemia (AML) induction therapy, are at risk of developing severe mucositis and diarrhea due to the damage chemotherapy inflicts on rapidly dividing cells, including those lining the GI tract. Palifermin has been demonstrated to be effective in reducing the incidence of severe diarrhea in patients undergoing induction therapy for AML. A study (Bradstock et al., Br J Haematol 2014) investigated the use of palifermin as prophylaxis against gastrointestinal toxicity after AML induction therapy. The study found that patients who received palifermin had a statistically significant lower rate of grades 3 and 4 gastrointestinal adverse events, primarily due to a reduction in severe diarrhea. While the primary endpoint of reducing grade 3 and 4 oral mucositis was not statistically significant, the study did show evidence of reduced rates of higher grades of oral mucositis in the palifermin arm as well. Incorrect Options: Option A- Zofran (ondansetron): Zofran is an antiemetic medication commonly used to prevent nausea and vomiting associated with chemotherapy. While it helps with nausea and vomiting, it doesn't directly address the issue of severe diarrhea or mucositis in patients undergoing intensive chemotherapy. Option B- Compazine (prochlorperazine): Compazine is also an antiemetic medication that can help manage nausea and vomiting. Like Zofran, it doesn't specifically target mucositis or diarrhea. Option C- Imodium (loperamide): Imodium is an antidiarrheal medication that can be used to manage diarrhea. While it can be helpful in controlling diarrhea symptoms, it doesn't address the underlying issue of mucositis or prevent severe diarrhea in patients undergoing intensive chemotherapy. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 32-year-old female, Rh negative, after an RTA had required more than 20 units of blood. She was given type O blood, with some units that were Rh positive. 2 months later she consults you to discuss future pregnancy planning. Her current partner is Rh positive. What is the ideal mode of management?
questions.stemHtml: A 32-year-old female, Rh negative, after an RTA had required more than 20 units of blood. She was given type O blood, with some units that were Rh positive. 2 months later she consults you to discuss future pregnancy planning. Her current partner is Rh positive. What is the ideal mode of management?

options.label: A
options.text: Check serum for anti-IgG Rh anti-body

options.label: B
options.text: Give a dose of anti- Rh immunoglobulin

options.label: C
options.text: Confirm the Rh status of the partner

questions.answerText: Give a dose of anti- Rh immunoglobulin
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Give a dose of anti- Rh immunoglobulin: In Rh-negative women who have been exposed to Rh-positive blood, such as through transfusion or pregnancy with an Rh-positive fetus, there is a risk of developing Rh sensitization. Rh sensitization can lead to the production of antibodies against Rh-positive blood, which can be a significant concern in future pregnancies. To prevent this, a dose of anti-Rh immunoglobulin (Rhogam) is administered to the Rh-negative woman. This immunoglobulin binds to any Rh-positive blood cells that might have entered her bloodstream, preventing her immune system from reacting to them and thus reducing the risk of sensitization. This is particularly important when the woman is planning future pregnancies with an Rh-positive partner to prevent the development of HDN in the newborn. Incorrect Options: Option A - Check serum for anti-IgG Rh anti-body: Checking serum for anti-IgG Rh antibody is not the ideal approach in this situation. The goal is to prevent Rh sensitization, and waiting for the development of antibodies could lead to complications in future pregnancies. Option C - Confirm the Rh status of the partner: Confirming the Rh status of the partner is important, but regardless of the partner's Rh status, if the woman is Rh-negative and has been exposed to Rh-positive blood, administration of anti-Rh immunoglobulin is recommended to prevent sensitization. Option D - No further intervention: No further intervention is not appropriate in this case. Rh sensitization can lead to hemolytic disease of the newborn (HDN) in future pregnancies, which can cause severe anemia and other complications in the baby. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 30-year-old male comes to the office due to weakness for one year. He also has experienced weight loss due to reduced appetite and intermittent diarrhoea. The patient has no history of any substance or tobacco abuse. The vital signs are normal, except blood pressure is 96/66 mmhg. The cardiopulmonary examination is normal. Laboratory result shows: Potassium = 5.4 mEq/L Sodium = 129 mEq/L 8 am cortisol = 7.2 mcg/dL (normal 5-223 mcg/dL) TSH = 2.4 mIU/L (0.5 to 5.0 mIU/L) Which of the following should be the next best step?
questions.stemHtml:
A 30-year-old male comes to the office due to weakness for one year. He also has experienced weight loss due to reduced appetite and intermittent diarrhoea. The patient has no history of any substance or tobacco abuse. The vital signs are normal, except blood pressure is 96/66 mmhg. The cardiopulmonary examination is normal. Laboratory result shows:
	Potassium = 5.4 mEq/L
	Sodium = 129 mEq/L
	8 am cortisol = 7.2 mcg/dL (normal 5-223 mcg/dL)
	TSH = 2.4 mIU/L (0.5 to 5.0 mIU/L)
Which of the following should be the next best step?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - ACTH stimulation test: The patient with weight loss hyponatremia, hyperglycemia and low normal cortisol level is most likely diagnosed with primary adrenal insufficiency. This condition is also called Addison’s disease. The main causes of this condition are autoimmune infections, e.g., tuberculosis, Cancer or adrenal haemorrhage. The common manifestations are weight loss, fatigue, weakness, and gastrointestinal systems like diarrhoea. Potentially due to volume depletion due to Aldosterone deficiency. Vitiligo and hyperpigmentation can also be associated. 8 am serum cortisol and plasma ACTH should be done to find the cause of adrenal insufficiency, e.g. a low cortisol level with a high ACTH level means primary adrenal sufficiency. Incorrect Options: Option A - An expressed 24-hour urine-free cortisone: Urinary cortisols are decreased in primary insufficiency, but this test has very low sensitivity. This test can be used for Cushing syndrome. Cortisol is formed in response to hypoglycemia. Option C - Insulin-induced hypoglycemia test: Insulin-induced hypoglycemia test is done when insulin is given to induce hypoglycemia and cortisol levels are measured, but this test can be dangerous for patients. Option D - Intravenous hydrocortisone: Intravenous hydrocortisone is used to treat the adrenal crisis. Adrenal crisis presents with fever and hemodynamically instability after any acute stressors e.g. trauma, surgery or infection. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Which of the following findings on brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is suggestive of spontaneous intracranial hypotension?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following findings on brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is suggestive of spontaneous intracranial hypotension?
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Flattening of the optic chiasm: Several findings on head MRI can help establish the diagnosis of intracranial hypotension. These include diffuse, non-nodular enhancement of the pachymeninges (without leptomeningeal enhancement); “sagging of the brain” which can result in descent of the cerebellar tonsils, flattening of the anterior pons, obliteration of the basal cisterns and flattening of the optic chiasm; subdural fluid collections; enlargement of the pituitary which can mimic pituitary tumor; engorgement of the cerebral venous sinuses; and decrease in the size of the ventricles. Incorrect Options: Option A - Leptomeningeal Enhancement: Leptomeningeal enhancement refers to the abnormal enhancement of the meninges (the membranes covering the brain and spinal cord) on imaging studies, typically seen as bright areas on contrast-enhanced MRI. While leptomeningeal enhancement can occur in various conditions, such as infections, inflammation, and certain cancers, it is not a specific finding that suggests spontaneous intracranial hypotension (SIH). Option B - Enlargement of the Basal Cisterns: Enlargement of the basal cisterns is not a typical finding in spontaneous intracranial hypotension. In fact, SIH is characterized by the leakage of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), leading to decreased CSF pressure and resultant brain sagging rather than enlargement of the basal cisterns. Option D - Flattening of the Pituitary: Flattening of the pituitary gland may be seen in cases of intracranial hypotension, but it is not as specific or characteristic as other findings. Spontaneous intracranial hypotension can lead to changes in brain structures, including the downward displacement of the brain ("brain sagging"), which can affect the pituitary gland's position. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 25-year-old male comes to the clinic due to episodic palpitations and fatigue for the last 2 weeks. Physical examination reveals tachycardia. An ECG is performed and shown below: Which of the following is the underlying pathology in this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 25-year-old male comes to the clinic due to episodic palpitations and fatigue for the last 2 weeks. Physical examination reveals tachycardia. An ECG is performed and shown below: Which of the following is the underlying pathology in this patient?

options.label: C
options.text: Ectopic foci in the left ventricle

options.label: D
options.text: Reentrant circuit in the right atrium

questions.answerText: Reentrant circuit in the right atrium
questions.solution: Correct Option D- Reentrant circuit in the right atrium: This patient with palpitations, fatigue, and an ECG showing a saw-tooth wave pattern is suggestive of Atrial flutter. Atrial flutter is an arrhythmia characterized by an ectopic re-entry circuit usually within the right atrium around the tricuspid annulus. ECG characteristics of atrial flutter include: Saw-tooth flutter waves Narrow complex tachycardia May be regular or irregular Can be associated with an AV block Management of atrial flutter is the same as atrial fibrillation: Rate control: Beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers, digoxin Rhythm control: Antiarrhythmics e.g. amiodarone Anticoagulation for thromboprophylaxis Definitive treatment involves catheter ablation of the ectopic foci near the tricuspid annulus. Incorrect Options: Option A- Myocardial ischemia: Myocardial infarction presents with chest pain radiating to the left arm and neck, diaphoresis and an impending sense of doom. In MI, ECG shows ST-segment elevations rather than sawtooth waves. This relatively young patient with no risk factors is unlikely to experience a myocardial infarction. Option B- Myocardial hypertrophy: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy can occur as a familial disease or secondary to hypertension. Patients usually complain of angina-like symptoms. ECG reveals an increased amplitude of the QRS complex rather than sawtooth waves. Option C- Ectopic foci in the left ventricle: Premature Ventricular Contractions are ectopic beats arising from the ventricle. An ECG shows a wide QRS complex that is not preceded by a P wave. @Neet_pg_bot

She has had occasional bouts of gingival and nasal bleeding throughout her life, but no major bleeding. She has a poor response to DDAVP but has never required factor replacement or blood products. VWF levels on admission are at 35 IU/dL. Which of the following options is most ideal for this patient?

options.label: A
options.text: VWF concentrate 60–80 IU/dL at delivery, then 40 to 60 IU per kilogram every 8 to 12 hours then daily for 3 to 5 days. Target vWF:RCO > 50 IU/dL

options.label: B
options.text: VWF concentrate 60–80 IU/dL at delivery, then 40 to 60 IU per kilogram every 8 to 12 hours then daily for 3 to 5 days. Target vWF:RCO > 100 IU/dL

options.label: C

questions.answerText: VWF concentrate 60–80 IU/dL at delivery, then 40 to 60 IU per kilogram every 8 to 12 hours then daily for 3 to 5 days. Target vWF:RCO > 50 IU/dL
questions.solution: Correct Option A - VWF concentrate 60–80 IU/dL at delivery, then 40 to 60 IU per kilogram every 8 to 12 hours then daily for 3 to 5 days. Target vWF:RCO > 50 IU/dL : For patients with a history of type 1 von Willebrand disease (VWD) who have a poor response to DDAVP, the most ideal treatment option for expectant delivery is VWF concentrate with the following regimen: VWF Concentrate: VWF concentrate is the preferred treatment choice for patients with VWD who require interventions with the aim of raising their VWF levels to appropriate levels for prevention of bleeding. This includes childbirth. Dosage Regimen: The recommended regimen is to maintain VWF levels at 60–80 IU/dL at the time of delivery. Following delivery, continue with a dosage of 40 to 60 IU per kilogram every 8 to 12 hours, and then switch to a daily regimen for 3 to 5 days. Target VWF:RCO: The target VWF:RCO (ristocetin cofactor activity) level should be greater than 50 IU/dL. This level provides an adequate hemostatic response and reduces the risk of bleeding. Early Initiation: There is no role for early initiation of VWF concentrate before delivery, as the focus is on maintaining appropriate VWF levels during and after the delivery. Incorrect Options: Option B - VWF concentrate 60–80 IU/dL at delivery, then 40 to 60 IU per kilogram every 8 to 12 hours then daily for 3 to 5 days. Target vWF:RCO > 100 IU/dL : While maintaining higher VWF levels (greater than 100 IU/dL) might seem like a more aggressive approach, the target VWF:RCO level of greater than 50 IU/dL is generally sufficient to prevent bleeding events in most patients. Option C - VWF concentrate 60–80 IU/dL 3 days prior to delivery, then 40 to 60 IU per kilogram every 2 to 4 hours then daily for 3 to 5 days. Target vWF:RCO > 100 IU/dL : Initiating VWF concentrate 3 days prior to delivery and continuing at an increased frequency (every 2 to 4 hours) might not be necessary in this case, as the patient does not have a history of major bleeding and is not known to require such intensive treatment. Option D - VWF concentrate 60–80 IU/dL 3 days prior to delivery, then 40 to 60 IU per kilogram every 2 to 4 hours then daily for 3 to 5 days. questions.solution: Correct Option D - Fluid resuscitation in sepsis should be guided by clinical response and hemodynamic parameters, rather than predetermined targets: This statement reflects the current standard of care in sepsis management. questions.stem: A 29-year-old man was admitted to the hospital for GI bleeding after taking steroids and NSAIDs for pericarditis. He was hemodynamically stable on admission but was found to have a Hb of 6.2 g/dL, for which he was transfused 2 units of RBCs in the ER. 20 min into transfusion of the second RBC unit, he develops a fever to 100.9° F with rigors. All other vital signs are completely stable. Physical examination is negative for any acute cardiopulmonary findings or lower extremity edema. He did not have any fevers, chills or infectious symptoms prior to admission. After terminating the transfusion, a blood bank work-up was sent, which came out negative for hemolysis, and a clerical check is negative for mistransfusion (i.e., ABO incompatibility between the donor and recipient is ruled out). A bacterial culture of the remaining blood product, which results several days later, is also negative. Which of the following interventions could have prevented this patient’s fever and rigors?

20 min into transfusion of the second RBC unit, he develops a fever to 100.9° F with rigors. All other vital signs are completely stable. After terminating the transfusion, a blood bank work-up was sent, which came out negative for hemolysis, and a clerical check is negative for mistransfusion (i.e., ABO incompatibility between the donor and recipient is ruled out). A bacterial culture of the remaining blood product, which results several days later, is also negative.

options.label: B
options.text: Pre-storage leukoreduction of the blood product

options.label: D
options.text: Prophylactic administration of acetaminophen prior to initiation of the transfusion

questions.answerText: Pre-storage leukoreduction of the blood product
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Pre-storage leukoreduction of the blood product: The clinical history, signs and symptoms are consistent with a febrile non-hemolytic transfusion reaction, which can occur with any blood product (although this reaction most commonly occurs with RBCs and platelets). Febrile non-hemolytic transfusion reactions occur due to the generation and accumulation of cytokines in stored blood products. Therefore, the risk of having a febrile non-hemolytic transfusion reaction positively correlates with increased number of leukocytes in the blood product, as well as the age of the blood product itself. Febrile non-hemolytic transfusion reactions are clinically characterized by the onset of fever (typically 1-2 degrees Celsius increase in body temperature from baseline), chills or rigors that occur 1-6 hours after initiation of the transfusion. A febrile non-hemolytic transfusion reaction is a diagnosis of exclusion, after other causes of fever in association with a transfusion (such as hemolysis and sepsis) have been ruled out. The primary strategy to prevent the onset of a febrile non-hemolytic transfusion reaction is prestorage leukoreduction of the blood product (answer choice B), which entails passing the cellular blood products through a filter during collection (apheresis) or shortly after collection to remove most of the leukocytes. In addition to reducing the risk of a febrile non-hemolytic transfusion reaction, leukoreduction also decreases the risk of graft rejection in transplant recipients and immune-mediated platelet destruction by minimizing exposure to HLA antigens present on transfused, donor leukocytes. Similarly, leukoreduction also decreases the risk of transfusion-transmitted CMV, as the CMV virus resides within white blood cells. Incorrect Options: Option A - Irradiation of the blood product: Irradiation of blood products causes DNA crosslinks, preventing the replication of lymphocytes without significantly damaging the function of RBCs, platelets or granulocytes. Irradiation of blood products prevents transfusion-associated GVHD in immunosuppressed individuals with deficient cellular immunity and in those receiving blood transfusions from a directed donor (first degree relative donor). Option C - Washing of the blood product: Washing of blood products (answer choice C) removes the plasma component of RBC and platelets. Washing is performed for individuals with IgA deficiency to prevent anaphylactic transfusion reactions mediated by anti-IgA antibodies of the IgE subtype, babies with neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenic purpura (NAIT) to wash out maternal anti-HPA-1a antibodies, and for some individuals with severe allergic transfusion reactions to plasma containing blood products. However, there is no role for washing to prevent the onset of febrile non-hemolytic transfusion reactions. Option D - Prophylactic administration of acetaminophen prior to initiation of the transfusion: Prophylactic treatment with acetaminophen (answer choice D) is incorrect, as this is not beneficial for preventing febrile non-hemolytic transfusion reactions. In a double-blinded randomized controlled trial, 315 hematology-oncology patients were randomized to receive either acetaminophen (500 mg) plus diphenhydramine (25 mg) versus placebo 30 minutes prior to transfusion, and monitored for 4 hours. There was no significant difference in the pretreatment and placebo groups with respect to transfusion reactions (1.4 versus 1.5 reactions per 100 transfusions, respectively) (Kennedy et al. Transfusion 2008). Similarly, another review of 6 studies also found no demonstrable benefit of pre-medication with acetaminophen and diphenhydramine to prevent transfusion reactions @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 38-year-old female, otherwise in good health, was driving with relatives when their vehicle got stuck in the sand. Later, the relatives found her unresponsive in the van. As she was pulled out, a strong smell of fumes was noticed. The paramedics noticed agitation and intubated her in the field. In less than 2 hours, the patient is taken to the ER of the nearby hospital. The oxygen saturation as measured by pulse oximeter is 100% on 100 percent oxygen. She is sedated. Her temperature is 98.0°F, pulse is 88/min, and BP is 121/86 mm of Hg. A co-oximeter measured carboxyhemoglobin (CO-Hb) level is 26%, and hyperbaric oxygen (HBO) therapy is considered. Which biochemical measurement is suggested as a marker of severity of poisoning?

Her temperature is 98.0°F, pulse is 88/min, and BP is 121/86 mm of Hg. A co-oximeter measured carboxyhemoglobin (CO-Hb) level is 26%, and hyperbaric oxygen (HBO) therapy is considered. Which biochemical measurement is suggested as a marker of severity of poisoning?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Lactate: CO-Hgb levels are likely positively correlated with initial lactate levels in carbon monoxide (CO) poisoning. Patients who received HBO treatment had elevated plasma lactate concentrations and additionally had more frequent altered mental status. Although HBO therapy is used in different settings, generally accepted indications for HBO treatment are the presence of significantly increased COHb values and neurologic or cardiac deterioration. However, a lactate value >1.85mmol/L can predict the need for HBO treatment, which could be taken as a measure of severe poisoning. Lactate levels are also increased in alcohol intoxication, salicylate poisoning, and paraquat poisoning. Incorrect Options: Option B - Carboxyhemoglobin (CO-Hgb): While carboxyhemoglobin levels are measured to confirm carbon monoxide (CO) poisoning and guide treatment decisions, it is not considered a marker of the severity of poisoning. CO-Hgb levels indicate the percentage of hemoglobin that is bound to carbon monoxide instead of oxygen. A high CO-Hgb level, as in this case (26%), confirms the diagnosis of CO poisoning, but it does not provide information about the severity of the poisoning or the degree of tissue hypoxia. The severity of CO poisoning is better assessed by clinical features, such as the patient's mental status, oxygen saturation, and the presence of symptoms like confusion, agitation, or altered consciousness. Option C - Creatinine: Creatinine levels are not used as a marker of severity in carbon monoxide poisoning. Creatinine is a waste product produced by muscles and excreted by the kidneys. It is commonly measured to assess kidney function and to estimate glomerular filtration rate (GFR). In cases of carbon monoxide poisoning, the focus is on assessing the extent of tissue hypoxia and damage caused by the lack of oxygen, rather than kidney function. Option D - Creatine phosphokinase (CrPK or CPK): Creatine phosphokinase (also known as creatine kinase or CPK) is an enzyme found in various tissues, including muscle and brain cells. Elevated CPK levels can indicate muscle damage, such as in muscle injuries, heart attacks, or rhabdomyolysis. However, CPK levels are not used as a marker of severity in carbon monoxide poisoning. The focus in CO poisoning is primarily on evaluating the extent of tissue hypoxia and its effects on the brain and other organs @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 65-year-old patient with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is prescribed long-term oxygen therapy (LTOT). Which of the following oxygen delivery devices is most commonly used for LTOT in patients with COPD?
questions.stemHtml: A 65-year-old patient with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is prescribed long-term oxygen therapy (LTOT). Which of the following oxygen delivery devices is most commonly used for LTOT in patients with COPD?
questions.solution: Correct Option D - Reservoir Nasal Cannula: Long-term oxygen therapy (LTOT) is often used in patients with chronic lung diseases, including COPD, to improve oxygenation. The most commonly used oxygen delivery device for LTOT in patients with COPD is the Reservoir Nasal Cannula. Reservoir Nasal Cannula, also known as the “Oxymizer” or “Mustache Cannula,” is designed to conserve oxygen by storing it in a reservoir bag, which reduces the overall oxygen flow rate required to maintain a target oxygen saturation (SpO 2 ) level. This device is well-tolerated by patients and is particularly useful for those who need oxygen therapy for extended periods. Incorrect Options: Option A - High-Flow Nasal Cannula: High-flow nasal cannulas are typically used for providing high-flow, humidified oxygen therapy to patients with various respiratory conditions. While they can be beneficial in certain COPD exacerbations, they are not the primary choice for long-term oxygen therapy. Option B - Simple Nasal Cannula: Simple nasal cannulas deliver low-flow oxygen and are commonly used for short-term oxygen therapy or during activities where the patient needs supplemental oxygen. They are not typically used for LTOT in COPD patients. Option C - Venturi Mask: Venturi masks are used to deliver controlled, precise FiO 2 levels and are often used in acute care settings. They are not a primary choice for LTOT in patients with COPD. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option D- Ischemic cardiomyopathy: Cardiomyopathy is a condition that affects the heart muscle, and ischemic cardiomyopathy is the most prevalent kind among older people. This kind of cardiomyopathy results in reduced heart muscle contractility because of a lack of blood flow and is brought on by coronary artery disease. Incorrect Options: Option A- Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy: Younger people are more frequently affected by hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, which is characterized by the thickening of the heart muscle, which reduces the size of the left ventricle and causes diastolic dysfunction. Option B- Dilated cardiomyopathy: An enlarged left ventricular cavity and diminished systolic function are the hallmarks of dilated cardiomyopathy, which is more frequently observed in younger patients. Option C- Restrictive cardiomyopathy: The heart's ability to fill properly is compromised in restrictive cardiomyopathy because the ventricular walls or the surrounding tissue are rigid. The elderly do not frequently exhibit it. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option C- Chronic alcohol abuse: A known risk factor for the onset of myocarditis is chronic alcohol usage. Chronic alcohol misuse can also impair immunity, leaving the body more vulnerable to illnesses resulting in myocarditis. questions.answerText: Oral prednisone for 10 days with eye care/protection
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Oral prednisone for 10 days with eye care/protection: This patient has Bell’s palsy, i.e., an idiopathic unilateral mononeuropathy of cranial nerve VII. Multiple oral steroid regimens (25 mg bid for 10 days, 60 mg for 5 days followed by a taper over 5 days) have proven beneficial (increase rate of recovery and degree of recovery) in RCTs. Incorrect Options: Option A - Five grams of IV methylprednisolone over 5 days with eye care/protection: While corticosteroids (such as methylprednisolone) are commonly used in the treatment of Bell's palsy, the patient's presentation and clinical course are not consistent with Bell's palsy. Bell's palsy typically presents with acute-onset, painless, unilateral facial weakness that reaches its peak within 48 hours and gradually improves over several weeks. In this case, the patient's clinical presentation is more suggestive of a different condition, and IV methylprednisolone is not the most appropriate treatment. Option B - Eye care/protection alone as steroids and/or antivirals would have no effect on the outcome if they were started this far out from onset: This option suggests that treatment with steroids and/or antivirals would not be effective if started one day after symptom onset. Option D - Valacyclovir for 10 days with eye care/protection: Valacyclovir is an antiviral medication commonly used to treat herpes simplex virus infections, including herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1) which can cause facial nerve palsy (Ramsay Hunt syndrome). Additionally, the presence of hyperacusis and altered taste on the right side of her tongue is not typically seen in Ramsay Hunt syndrome. Therefore, valacyclovir is not the most appropriate treatment in this case. Option E - Oral prednisone and valacyclovir for 10 days with eye care/protection: While combining oral prednisone and valacyclovir is a common approach in the treatment of Ramsay Hunt syndrome, this patient's clinical presentation does not strongly suggest a viral etiology. questions.stem: A 35-year-old female presents with edema, fatigue, and frothy urine. Blood tests show hypoalbuminemia and hyperlipidemia. Urinalysis shows proteinuria, with urine protein-to-creatinine ratio of 5. A kidney biopsy shows diffuse thickening of the glomerular basement membrane and spike-like projections on silver stain. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 35-year-old female presents with edema, fatigue, and frothy urine. Blood tests show hypoalbuminemia and hyperlipidemia. Urinalysis shows proteinuria, with urine protein-to-creatinine ratio of 5. A kidney biopsy shows diffuse thickening of the glomerular basement membrane and spike-like projections on silver stain. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Membranous nephropathy: Membranous nephropathy is a type of glomerulonephritis that affects the glomerular basement membrane (GBM) of the kidneys, leading to proteinuria and often nephrotic syndrome. It is a relatively common cause of nephrotic syndrome in adults, with an estimated incidence of 2-10 cases per million per year. The diagnosis of membranous nephropathy is typically made based on a combination of clinical presentation, laboratory tests, and kidney biopsy findings. The clinical presentation usually includes edema, proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, and hyperlipidemia. Urine tests will show significant proteinuria, often with a urine protein-to-creatinine ratio of greater than 3-4. Blood tests may show hypoalbuminemia and hyperlipidemia. Kidney biopsy is necessary to confirm the diagnosis of membranous nephropathy and to distinguish it from other types of glomerulonephritis. The biopsy findings in membranous nephropathy typically show diffuse thickening of the GBM, with subepithelial immune complex deposits that can be seen on electron microscopy. The deposits may appear as spike-like projections or as granular deposits. The glomeruli may also show evidence of mesangial expansion and interstitial fibrosis. Incorrect Options: Option A - Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis: Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (MPGN) is classified into three subtypes based on the location of the immune deposits within the glomeruli. These types include: Type I MPGN Type II MPGN (also known as dense deposit disease) Type III MPGN (also known as immune complex-mediated MPGN) Type I MPGN is the most common subtype and is characterized by subendothelial immune deposits, while type II MPGN is characterized by dense intramembranous deposits of complement component C3. Type III MPGN is rare and is characterized by subepithelial or intramembranous immune deposits. Option C - Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis: Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN) is a type of acute nephritic syndrome that occurs as a result of an immune response to a group A streptococcal infection, typically a pharyngeal or skin infection. PSGN is more common in children than in adults, and it typically resolves on its own within a few weeks to months. On biopsy, PSGN is characterized by diffuse endocapillary proliferation. There may also be neutrophil infiltration, fibrinoid necrosis, and a "lumpy-bumpy" appearance of the glomeruli due to the deposition of immune complexes. Immunofluorescence staining may show granular deposits of immunoglobulin G (IgG), immunoglobulin M (IgM), and C3 along the glomerular basement membrane. Option D - Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis: Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (RPGN) is a type of glomerulonephritis that progresses rapidly, usually over days to weeks, and can lead to severe renal impairment or even renal failure. There are several types of RPGN, biopsy findings show crescentic glomerulonephritis with other findings specific to each type. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stemHtml: A 1-year-old girl is brought to you with a 2-days history of high-grade fever and crying while passing urine. Two months ago, she was treated for pyelonephritis with cefixime. Her temperature is 39.2°C (102.6°F), and her pulse is 118/min. On examination, there is tenderness at the costovertebral junction. The urine dipstick shows leukocyte esterase; urinalysis shows WBCs. A micturating cystourethrogram shows vesicoureteral reflux. Without treatment, he Is likely to develop which of the following complication in the future?
questions.solution: Correct Option A: Chronic kidney disease The history of recurrent pyelonephritis in children is linked to vesicoureteral reflux, confirmed by a micturating cystourethrogram. Chronic kidney disease is a long-standing complication of untreated VUR Vesicoureteral reflux: The retrograde urine flow from the bladder into the ureter and kidneys is known as vesicoureteral reflux (VUR). Before developing a urinary tract infection, patients with VUR typically show no symptoms. The symptoms include fever, dysuria, burning micturition (crying while passing urine), urgency, and flank pain. The UTI is frequently recurrent. Complications Chronic kidney disease; long-standing untreated VUR can lead to the development of chronic kidney disease Chronic retrograde flow of urine caused by VUR increases the pressure within the lumen of the nephron. It dilates the renal calyces, leading to compression of the surrounding blood vessels, causing a decrease in the blood flow through these vessels and hypoperfusion of the kidneys. Ischemia of the renal parenchyma leads to atrophic changes in the kidney, which Is responsible for replacing the renal parenchyma with scar tissue. If VUR is left untreated, it will lead to progressive destruction of the nephron and renal scarring that ends up in the development of CKD. Secondly, chronic pyelonephritis also accelerates the progression of scarring and the development of CKD Other complications of VUR include urosepsis, perinephric abscess, and renal scarring. Incorrect options: Option B: Renal cell carcinoma VUR does not increase the risk of the development of renal cell carcinoma Von-Hippel Lindau syndrome is responsible for the development of RCC in children Option C: Ureteric stricture Vesicoureteral reflux leads to the development of hydroureter and hydronephrosis due to the retrograde flow of urine in the ureters and renal pelvis that elevates the pressure in the ureters and renal pelvis It does not give rise to ureteric stricture formation Option D: Nephrotic syndrome VUR does not increase the risk of nephrotic syndrome as the nephrotic syndrome is caused by diseases that damage the glomeruli The nephrotic syndrome manifests with proteinuria, body swellings, and hyperlipidemia @Neet_pg_bot

Correct Option A: Chronic kidney disease 

  • The history of recurrent pyelonephritis in children is linked to vesicoureteral reflux, confirmed by a micturating cystourethrogram.
  • Chronic kidney disease is a long-standing complication of untreated VUR

Vesicoureteral reflux: 

  • The retrograde urine flow from the bladder into the ureter and kidneys is known as vesicoureteral reflux (VUR).
  • Before developing a urinary tract infection, patients with VUR typically show no symptoms. The symptoms include fever, dysuria, burning micturition (crying while passing urine), urgency, and flank pain. The UTI is frequently recurrent. 

Complications 

  • Chronic kidney disease; long-standing untreated VUR can lead to the development of chronic kidney disease
    • Chronic retrograde flow of urine caused by VUR increases the pressure within the lumen of the nephron. It dilates the renal calyces, leading to compression of the surrounding blood vessels, causing a decrease in the blood flow through these vessels and hypoperfusion of the kidneys.
    • Ischemia of the renal parenchyma leads to atrophic changes in the kidney, which Is responsible for replacing the renal parenchyma with scar tissue. If VUR is left untreated, it will lead to progressive destruction of the nephron and renal scarring that ends up in the development of CKD.
    • Secondly, chronic pyelonephritis also accelerates the progression of scarring and the development of CKD
    • Other complications of VUR include urosepsis, perinephric abscess, and renal scarring.

Incorrect options:

Option B: Renal cell carcinoma 

  • VUR does not increase the risk of the development of renal cell carcinoma
  • Von-Hippel Lindau syndrome is responsible for the development of RCC in children

Option C: Ureteric stricture 

  • Vesicoureteral reflux leads to the development of hydroureter and hydronephrosis due to the retrograde flow of urine in the ureters and renal pelvis that elevates the pressure in the ureters and renal pelvis 
  • It does not give rise to ureteric stricture formation

Option D: Nephrotic syndrome 

  • VUR does not increase the risk of nephrotic syndrome as the nephrotic syndrome is caused by diseases that damage the glomeruli
  • The nephrotic syndrome manifests with proteinuria, body swellings, and hyperlipidemia

His medical history includes diabetes and hypertension. Laboratory investigations reveal elevated serum creatinine and blood urea nitrogen levels. questions.stemHtml: A 65-year-old male patient is admitted to the hospital with complaints of decreased urine output and swelling in his legs for the past 3 days. His medical history includes diabetes and hypertension. Laboratory investigations reveal elevated serum creatinine and blood urea nitrogen levels. Urine analysis shows the presence of casts and proteinuria. The patient is diagnosed with acute kidney injury (AKI). Which of the following is the appropriate treatment option for this patient?

options.label: A
options.text: Administration of a high dose of a loop diuretic

questions.solution: Correct Option B- Initiation of renal replacement therapy (RRT): The treatment of severe acute kidney injury (AKI) involves aggressive management of the underlying cause and supportive care to maintain vital organ function. The initial management of AKI includes hemodynamic stabilization, which is achieved through fluid resuscitation and correction of electrolyte abnormalities. In cases of severe AKI, renal replacement therapy (RRT) may be required to replace the kidney's filtration function. There are two types of RRT: haemodialysis and peritoneal dialysis. Hemodialysis is the most common form of RRT, which involves the use of an external machine to filter blood through a semipermeable membrane. Peritoneal dialysis, on the other hand, involves the installation of a special solution into the abdominal cavity, which helps to remove excess fluid and waste products from the body. In addition to RRT, other treatments may be necessary to manage the underlying cause of AKI. For example, antibiotics may be given for infections, and medication adjustments may be made for patients with drug-induced AKI. Close monitoring and management of complications, such as electrolyte imbalances, acidosis, and fluid overload, are also essential components of the treatment of severe AKI. Incorrect Options: Option A- Administration of a high dose of a loop diuretic: Loop diuretics are commonly used in the management of fluid overload in AKI. However, in cases of severe AKI, where the kidney function is severely compromised, loop diuretics may not be effective in reducing fluid overload. Moreover, high doses of loop diuretics may lead to electrolyte imbalances, such as hypokalemia and hyponatremia. Option C- Empiric antibiotic therapy: Antibiotic therapy is not a standard treatment option for AKI. Although AKI can be caused by infections, such as pyelonephritis or sepsis, antibiotics are only used in these cases. Empiric antibiotic therapy can lead to the development of antibiotic resistance and adverse effects, such as diarrhoea and allergic reactions. Option D- Intravenous infusion of 0.9% saline: Intravenous infusion of 0.9% saline is used in the management of hypovolemia and dehydration. However, in cases of AKI, the administration of 0.9% saline can lead to volume overload and exacerbate the condition. The use of intravenous fluids is guided by the patient's fluid status and electrolyte levels, and excessive fluid administration should be avoided. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option D - He should undergo endoscopic mucosal resection: The next step in management in a patient with Barrett's esophagus who is found to have dysplasia within a "short" (<3 cm) Barrett's segment or intramucosal carcinoma in a biopsy, is to perform staging studies (further biopsies, generally at every 1 cm), followed by endoscopic mucosal resection (EMR). Incorrect Options: Option A - He should continue to undergo surveillance endoscopy to see if this develops into carcinoma: This option is incorrect because dysplasia in Barrett's esophagus is considered a precancerous condition. When dysplasia is identified, it indicates an increased risk of developing esophageal carcinoma (cancer). As such, continued surveillance is not the appropriate course of action. Intervention is required to prevent the progression to carcinoma. Option B - He should undergo radiofrequency ablation therapy: This option is incorrect because radiofrequency ablation (RFA) therapy is typically used for the treatment of Barrett's esophagus with low-grade dysplasia or high-grade dysplasia that does not involve any visible cancer (carcinoma in situ). In this case, the patient has dysplasia on several histologic specimens, which may indicate a more advanced stage than what RFA can address. Endoscopic mucosal resection (EMR) or other treatments might be more suitable. Option C - He should undergo photodynamic therapy: This option is incorrect because photodynamic therapy (PDT) is used for treating high-grade dysplasia or early-stage esophageal carcinoma that is limited to the superficial layers of the esophagus (also known as intramucosal carcinoma). In this case, the patient has dysplasia but no visible mucosal irregularities, which suggests that PDT may not be the most appropriate treatment. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man presented in the emergency department with breathlessness, palpitations, fatigue and mild chest pain. He binged on alcohol a few hours ago. Which of the following would be the likely cause of his presentation?
questions.stemHtml: A 50-year-old man presented in the emergency department with breathlessness, palpitations, fatigue and mild chest pain. He binged on alcohol a few hours ago. Which of the following would be the likely cause of his presentation?
questions.solution: Correct Option A- Atrial fibrillation: The patient's presentation and ECG findings are consistent with atrial fibrillation. Alcohol is one of the common causes of atrial fibrillation. Atrial fibrillation is a type of complex arrhythmia that constitutes both automatic abnormal firing and the presence of many reentry circuits that loops around the atria. Atrial fibrillation episodes arise from ectopic beats that originate from the conducting tissue in the damaged atrial tissue or the pulmonary veins . The characteristic features of the ECG include irregularly irregular rhythm, irregular QRS complexes and absent p waves. Atrial fibrillation can be of two types: Paroxysmal atrial fibrillation : In this type, patients will have intermittent episodes of the AF that will self-terminate in 7 days . Treatment: No treatment is needed if the patients have occasional well-tolerated attacks . Beta-blockers are the first line of treatment in symptomatic patients . Persistent atrial fibrillation: In this type of AF, the patient will have a prolonged episode that will only terminate with pharmacological or electrical cardioversion or remain permanent . Treatment includes two options: Rhythm control with either electrical or pharmacological cardioversion. Rate control with beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers or digoxin. Incorrect Options: Option B- First-degree heart block: The ECG of this patient is inconsistent with first-degree heart block. There will be a delay in AV conduction in first-degree heart block. The PR interval will be prolonged on the ECG . It would be longer than 0.20 seconds. There is no need for treatment. Option C- Torsades de pointes: Torsades de pointes is a type of polymorphic ventricular tachycardia . It happens as a result of a prolonged QT interval caused by prolonged ventricular repolarization. The ECG will show rapid irregular complexes that twist around the baseline as the QRS axis changes. During sinus rhythm, there will be a prolonged QT interval (>0.46sec in women and >0.44sec in men). Torsades de pointes are more common in women and can be triggered by medications and electrolyte disturbances, causing the QT interval to lengthen. Option D- Sick sinus syndrome: Sick sinus syndrome is more common in older people but can also occur in children. Ischemia, fibrosis, or degenerative changes in the SA node commonly cause sick sinus syndrome. The patient presents with palpitations, dizzy spells, and syncope due to intermittent tachycardia and bradycardia. No ventricular or atrial activity on the ECG causing either Sinus arrest or SA block. This patient's symptoms and the ECG findings are inconsistent with sick sinus syndrome. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 25-year-old man is brought to the outpatient department because of behavioural changes over the past year. He has been experiencing bouts of depression and hearing voices. He has also developed a tremor in his left hand over the same period that has been worsening lately. Eye examination reveals findings shown in the following photograph. This patient is most likely to have which of the following findings?
questions.stemHtml: A 25-year-old man is brought to the outpatient department because of behavioural changes over the past year. He has been experiencing bouts of depression and hearing voices. He has also developed a tremor in his left hand over the same period that has been worsening lately. Examination reveals hepatosplenomegaly, broad-based gait and a low-frequency tremor that is more prominent in left hand. Sensory examination is unremarkable. Eye examination reveals findings shown in the following photograph. This patient is most likely to have which of the following findings?

options.label: D

questions.solution: Correct Option B - Low serum ceruloplasmin levels: The patient's depression, psychosis (hearing voices), tremor and gait disturbance combined with the characteristic eye finding of Keyser-Fleisher rings, suggests Wilson disease. Wilson's disease is an autosomal recessive genetic disorder caused by a mutation in the ATP7B gene. ATP7B is a copper-transporting protein that is primarily expressed in the liver, where it facilitates the incorporation of copper into ceruloplasmin, a copper-containing protein that is secreted into the blood. Defective ATP7B gene results in defective copper transport and metabolism that leads to copper accumulation in liver leading to cirrhosis. Copper is subsequently deposited in other organs, primarily the basal ganglia in the brain causing neurological dysfunction such as tremors, gait dysfunction, depression and psychosis. Inability of defective ATP7B protein to incorporate copper into apoceruloplasmin leads to low serum ceruloplasmin concentration. Low serum ceruloplasmin is diagnostic for Wilson disease. Incorrect Options: Option A - High serum ferritin: Elevated serum ferritin levels are a common finding in hemochromatosis that can lead to hepatosplenomegaly and signs of liver failure, as well as neurological symptoms if hepatic encephalopathy develops. However, the presence of ascites or peripheral edema would be expected in cases of chronic liver disease. Additionally, hemochromatosis typically presents in patients over 30 years of age and may involve other features, such as skin pigmentation, joint pain, diabetes, and cardiomyopathy and testicular atrophy in males. Option C - Elevated number of CAG repeats: Having an elevated number of CAG repeats on genetic testing is diagnostic of Huntington's disease (HD), which can result in impaired motor abilities such as gait disturbance and tremors. Typical clinical features of HD, including chorea, athetosis, sensory deficits, and autonomic symptoms like sweating and urinary problems, are not present in this patient. Moreover, HD does not affect the liver. Option D - Enlarged ventricles on CT scan of the brain: Enlarged ventricles on brain imaging is indicative of hydrocephalus. Normal pressure hydrocephalus mostly occurs in older individuals and is often associated with difficulty walking. However, since this patient does not exhibit other typical symptoms of NPH like dementia or urinary incontinence, it is less likely to be the underlying cause. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 35-year-old male notices haematuria of 3 days duration. O/E- icteric and mild abdominal diffuse tenderness, vitals are stable. Lab evaluation demonstrates anaemia, reticulocytosis, decreased haptoglobin, and elevated LDH and bilirubin. To further evaluate his condition, you proceed with flow-cytometry which demonstrates an absence of CD55 and CD59. Which bone marrow disorder is most closely related to the patient's underlying condition?
questions.stemHtml: A 35-year-old male notices haematuria of 3 days duration. O/E- icteric and mild abdominal diffuse tenderness, vitals are stable. Lab evaluation demonstrates anaemia, reticulocytosis, decreased haptoglobin, and elevated LDH and bilirubin. To further evaluate his condition, you proceed with flow-cytometry which demonstrates an absence of CD55 and CD59. questions.solution: Correct Option C - Aplastic anaemia: Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria (PNH) is an unusual condition with patients typically presenting in their 30s. The genetic underpinning of this condition is an acquired somatic mutation of the PIGA gene (Phosphatidylinositol Glycan class A) on the X chromosome. The protein product of the PIGA gene is involved in the creation of the glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI) anchor which serves to attach cell surface proteins to the cell membrane. Without the GPI anchor for protein attachment, these cells are prone to both intravascular haemolysis (lack of CD59) and extravascular haemolysis (lack of CD55). Clinical symptoms typically include erectile dysfunction, abdominal pain, (these smooth muscle symptoms are thought to be secondary to a decreased amount of nitric oxide caused by free haemoglobin during haemolysis) profound fatigue, and haematuria (see intravascular haemolysis above) especially during night-time hours. Thrombosis (large abdominal vein) is common in this patient population as free haemoglobin is associated with a pro-thrombotic milieu. Laboratory abnormalities include: high levels of LDH, low levels of haptoglobin, unbound haemoglobin in the urine, anaemia, reticulocytosis, with a negative direct ant globin test (Coombs test). The diagnosis can be confirmed using flow cytometry. PNH and aplastic anaemia are often found in tandem (this occurs in greater than 50% of cases). Although not completely understood, the underlying mechanism appears to be immune escape by PNH cells and subsequent proliferation in the setting on aplastic anaemia Incorrect Options: Option A - Chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML): CML is a type of cancer that starts in certain blood-forming cells of the bone marrow. It is characterized by a specific genetic abnormality in the cancer cells, the Philadelphia chromosome. CML would not explain the absence of CD55 and CD59 as seen in PNH. Option B - Myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS): MDS refers to a group of diverse bone marrow disorders in which the bone marrow does not produce enough healthy blood cells. While MDS might cause anaemia and other blood-related symptoms, the absence of CD55 and CD59, as well as the patient's overall clinical picture, are more consistent with PNH than with MDS. Option D - Fanconi's anaemia: Fanconi's anaemia is a rare inherited bone marrow failure syndrome that is characterized by physical abnormalities, bone marrow failure, and a higher risk of cancer. The genetic basis and clinical presentation differ from those of PNH. The described findings and clinical picture, such as the absence of CD55 and CD59, are not typical for Fanconi's anaemia. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: What is the mechanism of action of vigabatrin?
questions.stemHtml: What is the mechanism of action of vigabatrin?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Inhibition of GABA transaminase: Vigabatrin works through irreversible inhibition of GABA transaminase, decreasing GABA breakdown. Tiagabine inhibits the GABA transporter, leaving more GABA in the extracellular space following synaptic vesicular release. Barbiturates, 1,4-benzodiazepines, and the 1,5-benzodiazepine clobazam directly bind to and potentiate the GABA-A receptor. Incorrect Options: Option B - Sodium channel blocker: Vigabatrin does not directly block sodium channels. Sodium channel blockers are a class of medications that primarily target voltage-gated sodium channels to reduce neuronal excitability and are used in the treatment of epilepsy and other neurological conditions. Option C - Calcium channel blocker: Vigabatrin does not block calcium channels. Calcium channel blockers are a different class of medications that block voltage-gated calcium channels, which can reduce calcium influx into neurons and affect neurotransmitter release. Option D - Inhibition of GABA transporter: Vigabatrin does not inhibit the GABA transporter. GABA transporters are responsible for the reuptake of GABA (gamma-aminobutyric acid) from the synapse, regulating its concentration in the synaptic cleft. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option B - It is an inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase inhibitor: Mycophenolate mofetil is an immunosuppressant agent used as a steroid sparing agent in many neurologic disorders, including neuromyelitis optica. It is a noncompetitive, reversible inhibitor of inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase (IMPDH), an important enzyme in de novo purine synthesis. Guanosine monophosphate (the product of IMPDH acting on IMP) is not available in adequate amounts via the salvage pathway in lymphocytes. For this reason, the cytostatic effects of the drug are more lymphocyte selective (i.e., target tissue specific) than other steroid sparing agents. Option C - It acts as an analog of endogenous purines: it is the MOA of azathioprine (6-mercaptopurine). Option D - It is a calcineurin inhibitor: It is the MOA of cyclosporine A, Tacrolimus. Option E - It is a DNA alkylating agent: it is the MOA of cyclophosphamide. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.answerText: Mitral valve opens, and aortic valve closes
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Mitral valve opens, and the aortic valve closes: The right atrial pressure waveform monitors pressure changes produced during the cardiac cycle. 'a'-wave is a pressure wave that is produced when atria are depolarized. (when atria contracts). As a result of atrial contraction, pressure increases in the atria that forces the blood to the ventricle; this opens up both the AV valves i.e. mitral and the tricuspid valves. The only feasible option among the given option s is option "C." Incorrect Options: Option A - Mitral valve closes, and the aortic valve opens: This happens during the early systole when the ventricle contracts pressure in the ventricle gets higher than the atria. When the mitral valve opens the aortic valve closes and vice versa. Option D - Mitral valve close and aortic valve close: This is against the normal physiology of the heart. Both mitral and aortic valves cannot be closed at the same time. When the mitral valve opens the aortic valve closes and vice versa. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 35-year-old male presents with a right sided hydrothorax. The pleural fluid is drained and sent for pathological analysis. The patient has a recent history of a family member who had contracted tuberculosis. Which of the following characteristics of the pleural fluid would be characteristic of infection with Mycobacterium tuberculosis?
questions.stemHtml: A 35-year-old male presents with a right sided hydrothorax. The pleural fluid is drained and sent for pathological analysis. The patient has a recent history of a family member who had contracted tuberculosis. Which of the following characteristics of the pleural fluid would be characteristic of infection with Mycobacterium tuberculosis?
questions.solution: Correct Options A - Adenosine deaminase (ADA) > 40 U/L: Tuberculosis may present with pleural effusions, which characteristically are composed of a majority of lymphocytes. ADA positivity > 40 U/L makes the infection with tuberculosis more likely, though the finding may be found in malignancies and chronic inflammation. Incorrect Options: Option B - pH < 7.2, lactate dehydrogenase (LD) > 700, and glucose <30: These findings are characteristic of a pleural effusion due to rheumatoid arthritis. These parameters indicate a severe systemic inflammatory response which is not typically associated with tuberculosis. Option C - pH < 6.0: This is an unusually low pH for any type of pleural effusion and is more typically associated with an esophageal perforation leading to the leakage of gastric contents into the pleural space. This is not a typical finding in tuberculosis. Option D - pH < 7.2 with >100,000 neutrophils/mL: This is indicative of a purulent infection, or empyema, in the pleural space. While tuberculosis is an infection, it typically does not cause a purulent effusion and instead leads to a lymphocytic exudative effusion. Therefore, a high neutrophil count is not typically associated with tuberculosis. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 38-year-old female is evaluated for periodic episodes of nausea and mild to moderate nonspecific right sided abdominal pain. Transabdominal ultrasound of the right upper quadrant reveals gallbladder sludge, with a 5 mm hyperechoic mass projecting into the gallbladder lumen. Which of the following is appropriate for management?
questions.stemHtml: A 38-year-old female is evaluated for periodic episodes of nausea and mild to moderate nonspecific right sided abdominal pain. Transabdominal ultrasound of the right upper quadrant reveals gallbladder sludge, with a 5 mm hyperechoic mass projecting into the gallbladder lumen. Which of the following is appropriate for management?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Follow-up ultrasound in 6 months: Gallbladder polyps are commonly found on routine abdominal ultrasound. In most cases, they are benign polyps, but some will progress to gallbladder cancer. Management of gallbladder polyps is based on available evidence of clinical characteristics that suggest increased risk for malignancy. Patient risk factors for malignant polyps include age over 60, presence of gallstones, and primary sclerosing cholangitis. Polyp characteristics associated with higher risk are sessile morphology, size over 6 mm, and solitary polyps. Patients with polyps who have symptoms that are suggestive of biliary colic should generally undergo cholecystectomy. This patient has non-specific symptoms and a polyp that is 5 mm. Although there is no consensus on the time to follow-up, some experts recommend an initial follow-up at 3 months for polyps 6-9 mm in asymptomatic patients without signs of malignancy. At that time, if no significant change is noted, follow- up in 12 months is recommended. This patient has non-specific symptoms and can undergo follow-up in 6 months. Incorrect Options: Option B - Laparoscopic cholecystectomy: Fast-growing polyps, polyps that are wide-based, sessile, or have long pedicles, and those in patients over 50 or with concurrent gallstones are indications for cholecystectomy. Polyps between 10-20 mm in diameter should be regarded as possibly malignant, and a cholecystectomy with full thickness dissection is recommended. Option C - Obtain CEA and CA 19-9: Tumor marker levels are not useful for differentiating malignant and benign polyps. Option D - Open cholecystectomy: In patients with polyps greater than 18 mm in size, open cholecystectomy is indicated. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option C - Propylthiouracil (PTU): Pleural fluid eosinophilia by definition contains > 10 % eosinophils and may occur with a number of pulmonary conditions which may introduce air or blood into the pleural space, neoplasms, and infections. Drugs are also a plausible cause, as there are 25 drugs which are associated with development of eosinophilic pleural effusions, the most common drugs being PTU, sulfasalazine, and warfarin. The appearance from the time of initiating the drug and the effusion is typically two months. Treatment consists of discontinuing the offending agent and administering oral glucocorticoids. Incorrect Options: Option A - Fluoxetine: This selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) used for depression is not typically associated with eosinophilic pleural effusions. Its most common side effects include nausea, upset stomach, diarrhea, dry mouth, sleep problems, and weight changes. While drug-induced lupus can be associated with pleural effusion, fluoxetine is not typically implicated in this condition. Option B - Valproic acid: This medication is primarily used to treat epilepsy and bipolar disorder. While it can have numerous side effects, such as nausea, vomiting, dizziness, or tremor, it is not typically associated with eosinophilic pleural effusions. Option D - Clonazepam: This benzodiazepine medication is primarily used for treating anxiety and panic disorders, as well as certain types of seizures. questions.solution: Correct Option D – Artesunate: Malaria is among the most common protozoan diseases in the world. It is an endemic disease, but in the USA, travelers can exhibit symptoms. Additionally, there are endemic areas in the USA (Florida) where malaria can be contracted due to transmission from a mosquito bite. The pharmacological approach to malaria depends on the goal of the therapy. Prophylaxis is different when treating a regular infection versus a severe infection. Treatment for malaria should not be delayed until confirmatory testing is done. Clinical suspicion is enough reason to start treatment.
