questions.stem: A 45-year-old man presents to his primary care physician with complaints of headaches, palpitations, and sweating. His physician orders blood and urine tests to check for a potential hormonal disorder. The results reveal elevated levels of catecholamines and metanephrines, suggesting the presence of a pheochromocytoma. On genetic testing, he is diagnosed with Von Hippel-Lindau disease. Which additional screening test should be considered for a patient with pheochromocytoma and von Hippel-Lindau disease?
questions.stemHtml: A 45-year-old man presents to his primary care physician with complaints of headaches, palpitations, and sweating. His physician orders blood and urine tests to check for a potential hormonal disorder. The results reveal elevated levels of catecholamines and metanephrines, suggesting the presence of a pheochromocytoma. On genetic testing, he is diagnosed with Von Hippel-Lindau disease. Which additional screening test should be considered for a patient with pheochromocytoma and von Hippel-Lindau disease?
questions.solution: Correct Option D: Abdominal CT scan or MRI Von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) disease is a rare genetic disorder (autosomal dominant) due to mutations in the VHL gene on chromosome 3p26-p25. Individuals with VHL disease are at risk of hemangioblastomas, pheochromocytomas, and clear cell renal cell carcinoma. Individuals with von Hippel-Lindau disease have an increased risk of developing renal cell carcinoma (RCC), which is the most common tumor associated with this genetic disorder. Therefore, imaging studies such as a CT scan or MRI of the abdomen may be ordered to screen for RCC in this patient. Other imaging studies, such as retinal exams and brain MRIs, may also be considered depending on the patient's clinical presentation and symptoms. There is currently no cure for VHL disease, but treatment options are available to manage the symptoms and complications of the condition. These may include surgery, radiation therapy, medications, and regular monitoring to detect and manage any new tumors. Incorrect options: Option A: Bone density scan This is a test that uses X-rays to measure bone mineral density and assess the risk of osteoporosis and fractures. Bone density scans are not typically indicated for the screening of tumors associated with von Hippel-Lindau disease. Option B: Echocardiogram Echocardiograms are not typically indicated for the screening of tumors associated with von Hippel-Lindau disease, as the syndrome is primarily associated with tumours in the kidneys, adrenal glands, pancreas, and central nervous system. Option C: Colonoscopy Colonoscopies are not typically indicated for the screening of tumours associated with von Hippel-Lindau disease, as the syndrome is not typically associated with an increased risk of colon cancer. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option C - Oligoprogression refers to the clinical scenario where a few metastases progress, whereas all other metastases are stable or responding to a systemic therapy strategy The oligoprogressive phase is a relapsed phase of oligometastatic cancer after a cytoreductive treatment. (Alongi F, et al. Tumori. 2018) Oligoprogression refers to the clinical scenario where a few metastases progress, whereas all other metastases are stable or responding to a systemic therapy strategy. Unlike the oligometastatic state, there can be diffuse metastatic disease, therefore there is no upper limit about how many metastases a patient has. The key point is that with the exception of a few growing tumours, the majority of other tumours are not progressing Incorrect Options: Option A - The oligometastatic disease is a clinical diagnosis based on specific cut-offs of the number of metastases (usually up to 5) and involved sites (usually up to 5) The oligometastatic disease is an intermediate state between locally advanced and disseminated or multimetastatic cancer. A number of metastases limited to five lesions developed during follow-up after curative treatment of prostate cancer is significantly associated to better 5-year survival (73% vs. 43% of patients with more than five metastases). questions.stem: Pimavanserin has which of the following mechanisms of action?
questions.stemHtml: Pimavanserin has which of the following mechanisms of action?
questions.solution: Correct Option A: 5-HT2A inverse agonist: An imbalance between the serotonin and dopamine systems has long been implicated in the pathophysiology of Parkinson disease psychosis (PDP). An important discovery in the identification of a role for the serotonin system in PDP came from the identification of the agonist effect of the hallucinogen, lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD), on 5-HT2A receptors. Clozapine and quetiapine, in addition to their actions at D2 receptors, have antagonist properties at 5-HT2A receptors and are therefore two of the first line agents used in PDP. However, 5-HT2A receptors are constitutively active (in the absence of agonist). As a result inverse agonists at this receptor, such as pimavanserin, are more effective inhibitors of this receptor than are antagonists (like clozapine and quetiapine). Memantine, approved for use in advanced Alzheimer dementia, is a low affinity antagonist at the NMDA receptor antagonist. Histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitors, such as valproic acid which is used in the treatment of mania/bipolar disorder, have been shown to promote learning, memory, and have neuroprotective effects in animal models. Option D: Histone deacetylase inhibitor: Pimavanserin does not function as a histone deacetylase inhibitor. Its primary action is on the 5-HT2A receptor to modulate serotonin signaling. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Which of the following would not be associated with a false-positive or false-negative gastric emptying study?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following would not be associated with a false-positive or false-negative gastric emptying study?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Elevated hemoglobin A1c levels: While hyperglycemia at the time of the gastric emptying study can be associated with delayed gastric emptying and a false-positive gastric emptying study, a history of diabetes or an elevated hemoglobin A1c level with a normal blood glucose at the time of the study will not be associated with a false-positive test. Anticholinergic agents such as benztropine will also be associated with a false-positive study. However, domperidone, which is used to stimulate gastric motility (but is not approved for use in the United States), can lead to a false-negative gastric emptying study. Incorrect Options: Option A - Hyperglycemia: Hyperglycemia refers to high blood sugar levels, which can be associated with diabetes. While uncontrolled diabetes can lead to various complications, including gastrointestinal issues, it does not directly impact the results of a gastric emptying study. Hyperglycemia might exacerbate certain gastrointestinal symptoms, but it would not cause false-positive or false-negative results in the study. Option C - Domperidone: Domperidone is a medication used to treat nausea and vomiting. It works by increasing the movement or contractions of the stomach and intestines. If someone is taking domperidone during the gastric emptying study, it might influence the test results by affecting gastric motility. It could lead to false-negative results, where the study may show normal or faster gastric emptying due to the effects of the medication. Option D - Benztropine: Benztropine is an anticholinergic medication used to treat certain movement disorders and side effects of antipsychotic medications. It works by blocking the action of acetylcholine, a neurotransmitter in the nervous system. Anticholinergic drugs can slow down gastrointestinal motility, which could lead to delayed gastric emptying. Therefore, if someone is taking benztropine during the gastric emptying study, it might influence the test results and cause false-positive results, indicating delayed gastric emptying when it's primarily due to the medication's effects. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman with no known medical history presents to the emergency department for pain with eye movements and decreased vision in her right eye. She denies any recent viral illness or arthralgias. Over the past three months, she reports two episodes of intermittent diplopia and paresthesias in her right arm. Her ocular history is significant for contact lens use. She is a non-smoker. On exam, there is a relative afferent pupillary defect. Her vision is significantly decreased in the right eye with dyschromatopsia. Extraocular movements are full in both eyes but painful. Her fundoscopy appears normal. The remainder of her physical exam is significant for a positive Babinksi sign and absent tendon reflexes in both extremities. An MRI of the brain and orbit is ordered. Which of the following is most likely responsible for her ocular symptoms?
questions.stemHtml: A 28-year-old woman with no known medical history presents to the emergency department for pain with eye movements and decreased vision in her right eye. She denies any recent viral illness or arthralgias. Over the past three months, she reports two episodes of intermittent diplopia and paresthesias in her right arm. Her ocular history is significant for contact lens use. She is a non-smoker. On exam, there is a relative afferent pupillary defect. Her vision is significantly decreased in the right eye with dyschromatopsia. Extraocular movements are full in both eyes but painful. Her fundoscopy appears normal. The remainder of her physical exam is significant for a positive Babinksi sign and absent tendon reflexes in both extremities. An MRI of the brain and orbit is ordered. Which of the following is most likely responsible for her ocular symptoms?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Multiple sclerosis: The vignette describes a patient with likely optic neuritis . Optic neuritis can be secondary to multiple sclerosis or idiopathic . The patient’s history of a positive Babinski sign, absent tendon reflexes, and discrete episodes of paraesthesia and diplopia separated in time, are highly suggestive of multiple sclerosis. When this inflammatory demyelinating process affects the optic nerve, it is referred to as optic neuritis. An afferent pupillary defect and decrease in color vision are hallmarks of the disease. The afferent pupillary defect is determined by the swinging flashlight test. Light is directed toward the normal eye, and when the light is transitioned to the affected eye, the pupil will paradoxically dilate. This finding reflects damage to the optic nerve. On fundoscopy, the optic nerve can appear swollen or pale. On MRI imaging , fat suppressed T1 images will reveal contrast enhancement of the optic nerve. If suspicious for multiple sclerosis, coronal fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) MRI will eliminate signal from cerebrospinal fluid and bring out the periventricular high–signal intensity lesions diagnostic for multiple sclerosis. Treatment is with high dose IV methylprednisolone. Incorrect Options: Option B - Trigeminal neuralgia: Trigeminal neuralgia can be seen in multiple sclerosis (MS), and in some cases can be the first manifestation of MS. It is characterized by facial pain in the distribution of the trigeminal nerve. Patients develop severe pain with chewing and brushing. Treatment is often with carbamazepine and oxcarbazepine which are anticonvulsants used to slow nerve impulses. Option C - Acephalgic migraine: This form of migraine refers to visual aura without headache. Patients may report photopsias, nausea, occasionally hemiparesis, but lack the headache. Acephalgic migraines rarely last for longer than a few hours and are typically not associated with an afferent pupillary defect, since the pathology is not coming from the optic nerve. Option D - Syphilis: Syphilis is known as the “great imitator” due to its ability to mimic several ocular conditions with its varied presentation. Some cases of neurosyphilis have presented as an optic neuritis with rapid vision failure. However, the question asks for the most likely etiology of her symptoms, which is multiple sclerosis. @Neet_pg_bot

He reports that he has searched for possible causes of his symptoms online and is worried this is an early sign of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. Which of the following physical findings can help distinguish myasthenia gravis (MG) from amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS)?
questions.stemHtml: A 45-year-old male presents to the clinic with difficulty swallowing, which he states is worse as the day progresses. He reports that he has searched for possible causes of his symptoms online and is worried this is an early sign of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. Which of the following physical findings can help distinguish myasthenia gravis (MG) from amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS)?

options.label: A
options.text: MG lacks coexisting hyperreflexia with atrophy and fasciculations.

options.label: C
options.text: Dysarthria in ALS is never spastic.

questions.answerText: MG lacks coexisting hyperreflexia with atrophy and fasciculations.
questions.solution: Correct Option A - MG lacks coexisting hyperreflexia with atrophy and fasciculations: The distinction between MG and ALS may be difficult, particularly in the 6-9% of MG patients who are both anti-acetylcholine receptor antibody and MuSK-antibody negative. The diagnosis may also be challenging in rare patients with ALS who have fatigable limb weakness. Weakness (including neck extensors), dysphagia, and shortness of breath may be present in both patient populations. Certain physical examination features may aid in differentiating MG from ALS, as outlined in the following table. Clinical manifestations that distinguish ALS from MG are the presence of both upper motor neuron signs (hyperreflexia and Babinski signs) and lower motor neuron signs (hyporeflexia, atrophy, and fasciculations) in ALS, together with its progressive nature. Signs of Symptoms Amyotrophic lateral Sclerosis Myasthenia Gravis Muscle atrophy + - Fasciculations + - Hyperreflexia or hyporeflexia + - Ptosis - + Extraocular muscle weakness - + Reduced saccades + - Dysarthria Spastic and flaccid Flaccid, nasal speech Constipation + - Regurgitation of liquids or solids through nose - + Finger extensor weakness > intrinsic hand muscle weakness - + (+) = Present and (-) = Absent Incorrect Options: Option B - ALS demonstrates extraocular muscle weakness: Extraocular muscle weakness is not a characteristic feature of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). ALS primarily affects the motor neurons that control the voluntary muscles of the body, including those involved in speech, swallowing, and limb movement. While ALS can lead to weakness and atrophy of the muscles involved in eye movement, it is not a hallmark feature, and ocular symptoms are not a distinguishing factor between ALS and myasthenia gravis (MG). Option C - Dysarthria in ALS is never spastic: Dysarthria is a common feature in both ALS and myasthenia gravis (MG). Dysarthria refers to difficulty in speaking due to weak or uncoordinated muscles involved in speech production. In ALS, dysarthria can be either spastic or flaccid, depending on the involvement of upper motor neurons (UMN) or lower motor neurons (LMN). Spastic dysarthria occurs when there is damage to the UMN, whereas flaccid dysarthria is associated with damage to the LMN. Both types of dysarthria can be observed in ALS patients. Option D - Ptosis is present in ALS: Ptosis, which refers to drooping of the upper eyelid, is not a typical feature of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). Ptosis is commonly associated with myasthenia gravis (MG), especially when involving the ocular muscles. In MG, weakness and fatigue of the muscles, including those responsible for lifting the eyelids, can lead to ptosis. However, in ALS, ptosis is not characteristic, and the presence of ptosis would actually raise suspicion for myasthenia gravis rather than ALS. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 67-year-old guy with stable coronary artery disease visits the doctor for a checkup. Aside from the strange exertional chest pain he gets while cutting the grass or running for a long time, he feels good. He does 20 minutes of jogging once a week and uses a sublingual nitroglycerine tablet before his run to avoid sharp chest pain. The patient requested the doctor if he could increase the dose of the medication before running because he wanted to run farther distances. Which of the following outcomes is most probable when administering higher doses of this medication?
questions.stemHtml: A 67-year-old guy with stable coronary artery disease visits the doctor for a checkup. Aside from the strange exertional chest pain he gets while cutting the grass or running for a long time, he feels good. He does 20 minutes of jogging once a week and uses a sublingual nitroglycerine tablet before his run to avoid sharp chest pain. The patient requested the doctor if he could increase the dose of the medication before running because he wanted to run farther distances. Which of the following outcomes is most probable when administering higher doses of this medication?
questions.solution: Correct Option A- Reflex sympathetic activity: Low-dose nitrate increases myocardial perfusion mainly by reducing preload and acting as a vasodilator to decrease ventricular wall tension. High-dose nitrate also causes peripheral and coronary vessels to widen , which prevents coronary spasms and lowers ventricular afterload and, consequently, myocardial oxygen demand. Peripheral arterial dilation also contributes to systemic hypotension , which triggers a reflex sympathetic response that results in tachycardia and greater cardiac contractility. Myocardial oxygen demand consequently rises. Beta-blocker administration simultaneously has a synergistic anti-ischemic impact that can reduce reflex tachycardia. Incorrect Options: Option B- Rebound angina: When patients receive intermittent treatment, rebound angina occurs when their angina symptoms worsen due to drug levels dropping during the nitrate-free periods. Not sublingual delivery, but rather the use of transdermal nitroglycerin patches, is typically linked to it. Additionally, this patient has a minimal risk of rebound angina due to his once-weekly usage. Option C- Development of tolerance: Nitrate tolerance often develops after 2-3 days of continuous administration and is more probable with high dosages and long-acting preparations. Daily nitrate-free intervals of at least 8 hours are advised to reduce this adverse effect. A larger dosage won't increase the patient's risk of tolerance because he uses the drug only once every week, on average, and has enough time between doses. Option D- Anaphylactic reaction: Less than 1% of people receiving nitrate therapy experience anaphylactic reactions. Additionally, since the patient has been taking the medication consistently , an allergic response to a dosage increase is unlikely. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 54-year-old man visits his doctor for a check-up. He had an emergency heart catheterization three weeks ago due to a myocardial infarction. He was hospitalized for longer than anticipated due to decreased kidney function. The patient claims that his symptoms have improved considerably since then. He is now urinating considerably more than he was before the procedure. His serum creatinine is 1.6 mg/dL, and his blood urea nitrogen concentration is 20 mg/dL. Which of the following problems is this patient more likely to experience?
questions.stemHtml: A 54-year-old man visits his doctor for a check-up. He had an emergency heart catheterization three weeks ago due to a myocardial infarction. He was hospitalized for longer than anticipated due to decreased kidney function. The patient claims that his symptoms have improved considerably since then. He is now urinating considerably more than he was before the procedure. His serum creatinine is 1.6 mg/dL, and his blood urea nitrogen concentration is 20 mg/dL. Which of the following problems is this patient more likely to experience?
questions.solution: Correct Option A: Hypokalemia About two weeks after the initial event, acute kidney injury (AKI) patients typically recover full glomerular filtration function. However, tubular reabsorption is still impaired, leading to increased urine production and subsequent polyuria. Several electrolytes, such as potassium, sodium, and magnesium, that are typically reabsorbed by the tubules, are lost during the polyuric recovery period of AKI. Incorrect options: Option B: Hypernatremia This patient is in the polyuric recovery stage of AKI three weeks after exposure to contrast and is more at risk for hyponatremia than hypernatremia. Patients experience several electrolyte losses during this time, including sodium, which is typically reabsorbed by the tubules. Option C: Hyporeninemia Patients with AKI in the polyuric recovery phase are at risk for volume depletion, characterized by a decline in GFR and salt delivery to the distal nephrons and the subsequent release of renin. As a result, this patient would produce more renin. Option D: Metabolic alkalosis This patient's polyuric recovery phase of AKI has been present for three weeks following contrast exposure. Patients are at risk for metabolic acidosis rather than alkalosis during this time because they cannot excrete H+ ions and regenerate bicarbonate (both functions of the tubule system). @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option A - ACTH assay interference: In an SST, blood is first collected for baseline measurement of plasma cortisol and ACTH level. Then, 250 µg of Synacthen is administered intramuscularly, followed by measurement of cortisol levels at 30 and/or 60 minutes post-Synacthen. The cut-off for a normal cortisol response must be laboratory-specific or assay-specific (ranging from 420 to 574 nmol/L) due to variations among different cortisol assays. In this case, given the high plasma ACTH and borderline low cortisol levels, a short synacthen test (SST) was ordered, which showed normal serum cortisol levels post-Synacthen i.e. >550nmol/L, thereby excluding adrenal insufficiency. In cases of recent onset of secondary adrenal failure up to 4 weeks, it may produce a normal response to an SST but with low ACTH levels. However, in this case, the plasma ACTH that was repeated as part of the SST remained elevated at 40 pmol/L. This discordance between plasma ACTH and SST results should raise suspicion of ACTH assay interference. Measurement of plasma ACTH is an important step in determining the underlying cause of hypercortisolemia. Interfering substances in the immunoassays can lead to erroneous results impacting clinical management and leading to unnecessary investigations and interventions. Many hormones, including ACTH, are measured by immunoassays. The Siemens ACTH immulite assay is widely used in the labs, and has been reported to produce erroneously elevated results. Anything that affects the assay can cause falsely higher or lower results. For example, heterophile antibodies and macro-analyte. Heterophil antibodies are endogenous, weakly reactive antibodies that are found to be in 40% of the general population. A macro-analyte is an analyte bound to an immunoglobulin (e.g. macroprolactin or macro-TSH). It remains in the human circulation longer because of reduced clearance. Macro-analytes are biologically inactive but falsely elevate the result. Communication between physician and laboratory as well as appropriate investigations, including testing on an alternate platform using alternative analyser, serial dilution of sample and use of blocking antibodies, resulted in the identification of assay interference. If the result on an alternative analyser is similar to the initial result, and a serial dilution study shows linearity in the analyte concentrations with increasing dilution, assay interference is unlikely. On the other hand, a different result on an alternative analyser and non-linearity on serial dilution should lead to several more investigations, such as a heterophilic-blocking tube (HBT) study (to exclude heterophile antibodies interference) and a polyethylene glycol precipitation study (to exclude macro-analyte interference). ACTH secreting adenoma (Cushing’s disease), ectopic ACTH syndrome and ectopic CRH secretion are causes of ACTH dependent Cushing’s syndrome in which both ACTH and cortisol levels are high. Random cortisol measurements are unreliable. Highly indicative signs and symptoms such as facial plethora, proximal myopathy, reddish-purple striae, and easy bruisability should alert for biochemical evidence of Cushing’s syndrome through any of the first-line screening tests i.e. 24-hour urinary free cortisol, overnight dexamethasone suppression test, or late-night salivary cortisol. She is concerned about the risk of her child inheriting this condition. Which of the following statements regarding genomic imprinting is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Genomic imprinting is a process that affects only the mother's genes.

options.label: B
options.text: Imprinted genes always exhibit a dominant phenotype.

options.label: C
options.text: Angelman syndrome is typically caused by a paternally inherited deletion of the UBE3A gene.

options.label: D
options.text: Genomic imprinting is a reversible process that occurs throughout an individual's life.

questions.answerText: Angelman syndrome is typically caused by a paternally inherited deletion of the UBE3A gene.
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Angelman syndrome is typically caused by a paternally inherited deletion of the UBE3A gene: Genomic imprinting is an epigenetic phenomenon that involves the differential expression of genes depending on whether they are inherited from the mother or the father. In Angelman syndrome, there is typically a loss of function of the UBE3A gene located on the maternal allele. This means that the child inherits a deletion or mutation in the maternal allele of the UBE3A gene, leading to the characteristic features of Angelman syndrome. Incorrect Options: Option A - Genomic imprinting is a process that affects only the mother's genes: Genomic imprinting affects genes from both parents, not just the mother's genes. Option B - Imprinted genes always exhibit a dominant phenotype: Depending on the specific gene and its parental origin. Option D - Genomic imprinting is typically established during gametogenesis and remains stable throughout an individual's life: it is not a reversible process. @Neet_pg_bot

ECG reveals ST-segment elevation in leads II, III, and aVF. Transthoracic echocardiography shows an echo-free space around the heart. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A 54-year-old male presents to the emergency department with complaints of severe chest pain radiating to his left arm for the past 30 minutes. On examination, his blood pressure is 110/70 mmHg, pulse rate is 90 beats per minute, respiratory rate is 18 breaths per minute, and temperature is normal. ECG reveals ST-segment elevation in leads II, III, and aVF. Transthoracic echocardiography shows an echo-free space around the heart. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: Correct Option A- Pericarditis: The clinical scenario describes a 54-year-old male presenting with severe chest pain radiating to his left arm along with ST-segment elevation on ECG and echo-free space around the heart on echocardiography. This constellation of findings is most consistent with acute pericarditis. The pericardium is a double-layered sac that surrounds the heart and contains a small amount of fluid that lubricates the heart during its contractions. Acute pericarditis is an inflammatory condition of the pericardium that can cause severe chest pain , often radiating to the left arm, and ECG changes that mimic ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI). Echocardiography may reveal an echo-free space around the heart, indicating the presence of pericardial effusion. Incorrect Options: Option B- Myocardial infarction: Although ST-segment elevation on ECG is a hallmark finding of myocardial infarction (MI), the presence of an echo-free space around the heart on echocardiography suggests pericarditis rather than MI. Option C- Aortic dissection: Aortic dissection can cause severe chest pain but is usually accompanied by other symptoms such as unequal blood pressure in the arms , neurological deficits , or signs of ischemia in other organs. Echocardiography is not typically used to diagnose aortic dissection . Option D- Pulmonary embolism: Pulmonary embolism can cause chest pain, but it is typically associated with other symptoms such as shortness of breath and tachycardia . ECG changes and an echo-free space around the heart are not characteristic findings of pulmonary embolism. @Neet_pg_bot

He also reports chest discomfort and difficulty in breathing associated with these episodes. He says that holding his breath helps in controlling the symptoms. His medical history is significant for panic disorder for which he is undergoing cognitive behavioral therapy. Physical examination reveals regular tachycardia. An ECG is shown below. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A 23-year-old male comes to the clinic due to episodic palpitations and lightheadedness for the past couple of months. He also reports chest discomfort and difficulty in breathing associated with these episodes. He says that holding his breath helps in controlling the symptoms. His medical history is significant for panic disorder for which he is undergoing cognitive behavioral therapy. Physical examination reveals regular tachycardia. An ECG is shown below. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: Correct Option C- Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia (PSVT): This patient with palpitations and lightheadedness associated with chest discomfort and shortness of breath along with an ECG showing tachycardia with a narrow QRS complex and no P waves is suffering from PSVT AV nodal reentrant tachycardia (AVNRT) is the most common PSVT that is caused by re-entry of signals in a circuit involving the “fast” and “slow” pathways of the AV node ECG shows: Narrow complex tachycardia Regular R-R interval No discernable P waves P-waves may be buried within the QRS complex Clinical features include: Palpitations Lightheadedness Shortness of breath Diaphoresis Chest pain Incorrect Options: Option A- Atrial fibrillation: A-fib is characterized by abnormal ectopic bursts of activity arising from the tissue in the pulmonary veins or damaged myocardium in the atria ECG reveals no P waves, irregularly irregular rhythm, and chaotic fibrillary waves. Option B- Panic attack: A panic attack can present with palpitations, chest pain and shortness of breath, mimicking a cardiac event. However, physical examination and ECG is normal in a patient experiencing a panic attack. This patient with an abnormal ECG is more likely to be suffering from a PSVT. Option D- Ventricular fibrillation (V-fib): V-fib can lead to sudden cardiac death during acute myocardial infarction. It is characterized by an irregular chaotic rhythm with coarse waveforms of varying shapes and amplitude. @Neet_pg_bot

  • ECG shows:
    • Narrow complex tachycardia 
    • Regular R-R interval
    • No discernable P waves 
    • P-waves may be buried within the QRS complex

  • ECG reveals no P waves, irregularly irregular rhythm, and chaotic fibrillary waves.

  • A panic attack can present with palpitations, chest pain and shortness of breath, mimicking a cardiac event. 
  • However, physical examination and ECG is normal in a patient experiencing a panic attack. 
  • This patient with an abnormal ECG is more likely to be suffering from a PSVT.

Option D- Ventricular fibrillation (V-fib):

  • V-fib can lead to sudden cardiac death during acute myocardial infarction.
  • It is characterized by an irregular chaotic rhythm with coarse waveforms of varying shapes and amplitude.

questions.stem: A 36-year-old female (G4P2012) is transferred to the hospital for delivery. At 35 weeks of gestation, vaginal cultures tested positive for group B streptococcus, which is resistant to erythromycin. The patient has a history of allergies to penicillin, latex, and cephalosporins, which resulted in severe respiratory distress. Which of the following would be the most appropriate intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis for group B strep in this patient until her delivery?
questions.stemHtml: A 36-year-old female (G4P2012) is transferred to the hospital for delivery. At 35 weeks of gestation, vaginal cultures tested positive for group B streptococcus, which is resistant to erythromycin. The patient has a history of allergies to penicillin, latex, and cephalosporins, which resulted in severe respiratory distress. Which of the following would be the most appropriate intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis for group B strep in this patient until her delivery?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Vancomycin 1 g IV q 12 hours: Patients who receive vaginal cultures at the recommended window of 35-37 weeks gestation and are culture-positive for group B streptococcus should receive antibiotic prophylaxis for group B streptococcus during the delivery process. Due to the patient’s microbiology workup and medical history, the most appropriate choice would be vancomycin 1 g IV every 12 hours until the baby is delivered. Incorrect Options: Option A - Clindamycin 900 mg IV q 8 hours : Although the organism is sensitive to clindamycin, the fact that resistance to erythromycin is detected should cause hesitation in using clindamycin as prophylaxis due to the association with inducible clindamycin resistance. Option C - Cefazolin 1 g IV q 8 hours: It is also not the best choice as it is a cephalosporin-class antibiotic, and the patient has a history of allergy to cephalosporins. Option D - Ampicillin 1 g IV q 4 hours: Due to the patient’s history of allergies to penicillins and cephalosporins that resulted in respiratory distress, these agents should be avoided. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 23-year-old man presented to the emergency room with complaints of palpitations and discomfort while breathing for about 30 minutes while he was sitting in his office. Past medical history is significant for occasional palpitations but less severe than this episode. He does not have any chest pain, shortness of breath, or dizziness. On examination, pulse is notable for irregular rhythm, with a rate of 170 beats per minute. He is vitally stable. His ECG after controlling the rate is given below. Which of the following is the most likely complication his illness can lead to?
questions.stemHtml: A 23-year-old man presented to the emergency room with complaints of palpitations and discomfort while breathing for about 30 minutes while he was sitting in his office. Past medical history is significant for occasional palpitations but less severe than this episode. He does not have any chest pain, shortness of breath, or dizziness. On examination, pulse is notable for irregular rhythm, with a rate of 170 beats per minute. He is vitally stable. His ECG after controlling the rate is given below. Which of the following is the most likely complication his illness can lead to?
questions.solution: Correct Option B- Recurrent Supraventricular Tachycardia (SVT): The most likely diagnosis in this case scenario is Wolff-Parkinson White (WPW) Syndrome The given ECG shows: A sinus rhythm A rate of 75 beats per min Short PR interval Wide QRS complexes with a slurred delta wave This is consistent with WPW Syndrome. WPW syndrome is an arrhythmia caused by an accessory electrical pathway that bypasses the AV node. The condition is usually congenital and can be associated with other cardiac defects. Symptoms : Most people with WPW syndrome are asymptomatic and are termed to have the WPW pattern on ECG. Some experience a combination of these symptoms: palpitations, tachycardia, shortness of breath, lightheadedness, or syncope and are termed to have WPW syndrome. Diagnosis : ECG : An accessory pathway allows electrical impulses to reach the ventricles more rapidly. Hence causing the characteristic: short PR interval widened QRS complexes delta waves Once the diagnosis is confirmed, other tests are performed to assess the severity of the disease and heart function. Holter monitoring Electrophysiology study Echocardiography Treatment : Medical: Orthodromic AVRT: AV nodal blocking therapy via Vagal maneuvers or drugs such as Beta blockers, calcium channel blockers, Adenosine.[1] Antidromic AVRT and Afib with preexcitation: Rhythm control with procainamide or ibutilide. Catheter ablation : A procedure in which radiofrequency waves are used to destroy the accessory pathway. Surgical : In rare cases, surgery may be required to remove the accessory pathway. Complications : The most common complication of WPW syndrome is recurrent supraventricular tachycardia (SVT). Other complications include atrial fibrillation, atrial flutter, ventricular tachycardia, ventricular fibrillation, and heart failure. If left untreated, the arrhythmias from WPW syndrome can lead to hemodynamic instability, myocardial infarction and cardiac arrest . Incorrect Options: Options A- Ischemic Stroke: Ischemic stroke is the most common and significant complication of atrial fibrillation (AFib). Although the initial presentation of this patient was most likely due to AFib, it was originally caused by WPW Syndrome as shown in the ECG obtained after sinus rhythm was achieved. Atrial Fibrillation (AFib): In AFib, the disorganized electrical activity causes the atria to quiver instead of normal contraction, which can lead to blood stasis resulting in thrombus formation, stroke, or heart failure. Cause : Atrial Fibrillation can be caused by hypertension, coronary artery disease or myocardial ischemia, valvular defects or congenital heart defects . It can also be caused by an accessory tract such as in WPW which is termed Atrial Fibrillation with preexcitation. It can also be due to hyperthyroidism or other metabolic or endocrine imbalances . It can be due to certain drugs. It is important to find cause to formulate an appropriate management plan. Diagnosis : Electrocardiogram (ECG): Absent P waves Irregularly irregular ventricular rhythm : The disorganized electrical signals from atria cause the ventricles to contract at irregular intervals, hence causing an irregularly irregular rhythm on the ECG. It can be with or without a rapid ventricular response (RVR) Narrow or wide QRS complex : It depends on the underlying conditions of the heart. Holter monitoring: It is used to track cardiac electrical activity over a longer period of time to detect paroxysmal AFib. Echocardiogram to assess the structure and function of the heart. Blood tests: to check for underlying medical conditions or medication side effects. Treatment : Find and treat the underlying cause. Medications: Anticoagulants to prevent blood clots and decrease risk of stroke and Myocardial Infarction. Beta-blockers, or calcium channel blockers to control heart rate. If hemodynamically unstable or refractory to medical management , cardioversion to restore a normal heart rhythm. Ablation therapy to destroy abnormal scar tissue that may be the cause. Surgery , such as a maze procedure, to create scar tissue in the heart to redirect electrical signals. Complications : Stroke or thromboembolism due to impaired blood flow and stasis in the atrial pocket. Heart failure or cardiomyopathy due to prolonged periods of rapid or irregular heart rhythms Fatigue, shortness of breath, or chest pain due to decreased oxygen supply to the body. Option C- Myocardial Infarction (MI): MI occurs as a result of reduced blood flow to cardiac muscles. Any type of arrhythmia, if left untreated for a prolonged period, can cause fatigue and reduce the oxygen flow to cardiac muscles , hence resulting in MI. This is, however, not common as most arrhythmias are diagnosed at an earlier stage due to the appearance of other severe symptoms. Option D- Heart Failure: Arrhythmias can cause heart failure by causing it to pump inefficiently or irregularly , leading to decreased blood flow and oxygen supply to all of the body's organs and tissues. Atrial fibrillation (AFib) is a common arrhythmia that can contribute to the development of heart failure. Chronic arrhythmias that are not well-controlled can lead to structural changes in the heart over time, which can further impair the heart's function and contribute to heart failure. Treatment of arrhythmias either by medication, ablation therapy, or pacemaker implantation, can prevent or manage heart failure.​​​​​​​ @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 44-year-old gentleman, with intermediate risk FLT3 ITD AML who completed his third cycle of cytarabine consolidation coupled with midostaurin consolidation presenst to you for follow-up. You perform a bone marrow biopsy revealing no evidence of leukemia. Complete blood count is almost normal with a hemoglobin of 11.2 g/dL. What do you recommend at this time?
questions.stemHtml: A 44-year-old gentleman, with intermediate risk FLT3 ITD AML who completed his third cycle of cytarabine consolidation coupled with midostaurin consolidation presenst to you for follow-up. You perform a bone marrow biopsy revealing no evidence of leukemia. Complete blood count is almost normal with a hemoglobin of 11.2 g/dL. What do you recommend at this time?

options.label: A
options.text: Discontinue midostaurin and referral back for transplantation

options.label: B
options.text: Discontinue midostaurin and monitor with complete blood count every 3-4 weeks

options.label: C
options.text: Continue midostaurin for up to 1 year with CBC checks every 1-2 months

questions.answerText: Continue midostaurin for up to 1 year with CBC checks every 1-2 months
questions.solution: Correct Option C- Continue midostaurin for up to 1 year with CBC checks every 1-2 months: The use of midostaurin, especially in combination with standard chemotherapy, has shown to improve outcomes in patients with FLT3-mutated AML. Given that the patient has completed intensive chemotherapy and is in remission, continuing midostaurin serves as maintenance therapy to reduce the risk of relapse. Monitoring with CBC checks every 1-2 months is necessary to watch for any signs of relapse or complications. Incorrect Options: Option A- Discontinue midostaurin and referral back for transplantation: Allogeneic stem cell transplantation can be an effective treatment for patients with FLT3-mutated AML, especially if they have a high risk of relapse. However, in the given scenario, the patient is in remission after consolidation therapy. Simply discontinuing midostaurin and referring for transplant without evidence of relapse may expose the patient to the risks of transplantation without clear benefit. Option B- Discontinue midostaurin and monitor with complete blood count every 3-4 weeks While monitoring with CBC is essential, discontinuing midostaurin when the patient is in remission might risk an early relapse. Maintenance therapy with midostaurin can help prolong the duration of remission. Option D- Discontinue midostaurin and observe clinically Again, the risk here is discontinuing a drug that could potentially keep the patient in remission for longer. Solely observing the patient without regular CBC monitoring may delay the detection of a relapse. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 6-months-old girl is brought to the physician for follow-up after two episodes of urinary tract infections treated with antibiotics in the past 2 months. Her mother told that she developed an allergic reaction to sulfa antibiotics on her last visit. A voiding cystourethrogram is shown. Which of the following is the mechanism of action for the drug required to prevent long-term complications in this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 6-months-old girl is brought to the physician for follow-up after two episodes of urinary tract infections treated with antibiotics in the past 2 months. Her mother told that she developed an allergic reaction to sulfa antibiotics on her last visit. A voiding cystourethrogram is shown. Which of the following is the mechanism of action for the drug required to prevent long-term complications in this patient?

options.label: A
options.text: Inhibit cell wall synthesis by blocking peptidoglycan crosslinking

options.label: B
options.text: Inhibition of bacterial folic acid synthesis

options.label: C
options.text: Create free radicals to damage bacterial DNA

questions.answerText: Create free radicals to damage bacterial DNA
questions.solution: Correct Option: C Create free radicals to damage bacterial DNA Nitrofurantoin is used for antibiotic prophylaxis in children >3 months with vesicoureteral reflux who have shown an acute reaction following the administration of sulfonamide antibiotics. Nitrofurantoin is reduced to reactive intermediates by bacterial nitro reductases, which then attack ribosomal proteins, DNA and other molecules within the cell. Adverse effects GI (gastrointestinal) upset Hemolytic anemia in patients with glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency Peripheral neuropathy Liver toxicity Hepatitis Pulmonary fibrosis Contraindications Neonates< 01 month G6PD deficiency Pregnant women at term ( 38 to 42 weeks) During labor and delivery Impaired renal function( creatinine clearance < 60mL/min) Incorrect options: Option A: Inhibit cell wall synthesis by blocking peptidoglycan crosslinking Ampicillin and amoxicillin are less effective as prophylactic agents and are usually reserved for infants < 2 months of age. Option B: Inhibition of bacterial folic acid synthesis Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is a folic acid synthesis inhibitor and is used as a drug of choice for prophylactics management in children > 3 months with VUR; however, this patient has shown an allergic reaction following administration of a sulfa-containing antibiotic; therefore the use of TMP-SMZ is contraindicated. Option D: Inhibit 30S subunit of bacterial ribosomes Tetracyclines bind with the 30S subunit of ribosomes and inhibit bacterial protein synthesis. They are not recommended to be used for prophylaxis in children with VUR. They also cause tooth discoloration and enamel hypoplasia. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Correct Option: C Create free radicals to damage bacterial DNA

  • Nitrofurantoin is used for antibiotic prophylaxis in children >3 months with vesicoureteral reflux who have shown an acute reaction following the administration of sulfonamide antibiotics.
  • Nitrofurantoin is reduced to reactive intermediates by bacterial nitro reductases, which then attack ribosomal proteins, DNA and other molecules within the cell.

Adverse effects

  • GI (gastrointestinal) upset
  • Hemolytic anemia in patients with glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency
  • Peripheral neuropathy
  • Liver toxicity
  • Hepatitis
  • Pulmonary fibrosis

Contraindications

  • Neonates< 01 month
  • G6PD deficiency
  • Pregnant women at term ( 38 to 42 weeks)
  • During labor and delivery
  • Impaired renal function( creatinine clearance < 60mL/min)

Incorrect options:

Option A: Inhibit cell wall synthesis by blocking peptidoglycan crosslinking

  • Ampicillin and amoxicillin are less effective as prophylactic agents and are usually reserved for infants < 2 months of age.

Option B: Inhibition of bacterial folic acid synthesis

  • Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is a folic acid synthesis inhibitor and is used as a drug of choice for prophylactics management in children > 3 months with VUR; however, this patient has shown an allergic reaction following administration of a sulfa-containing antibiotic; therefore the use of TMP-SMZ is contraindicated.

Option D: Inhibit 30S subunit of bacterial ribosomes

  • Tetracyclines bind with the 30S subunit of ribosomes and inhibit bacterial protein synthesis. They are not recommended to be used for prophylaxis in children with VUR.
  • They also cause tooth discoloration and enamel hypoplasia.

questions.stem: A patent with metastatic colon cancer was started on treatment with FOLFOXIRI + bevacizumab. The surgeon has asked that treatment stop a few weeks before surgery. What is the half-life of bevacizumab?
questions.stemHtml: A patent with metastatic colon cancer was started on treatment with FOLFOXIRI + bevacizumab. The surgeon has asked that treatment stop a few weeks before surgery. What is the half-life of bevacizumab?
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Three weeks The half-life of bevacizumab is approximately 21 days. This means that it takes about 21 days for half of the drug to be cleared from the body. Given this half-life, if a surgical procedure is planned, the last dose of bevacizumab should preferably be given no sooner than 6 weeks before the surgery. This allows enough time for the drug to be eliminated from the body to reduce the risk of excessive bleeding during the surgery. Incorrect Options: Option A - One week: This is not the correct answer. The half-life of bevacizumab is longer than one week, as mentioned earlier, it is approximately 21 days. Option B - Two weeks: This is also not the correct answer. The half-life of bevacizumab is longer than two weeks. Option D - Six weeks: This is the correct time frame for stopping bevacizumab treatment before surgery. The half-life of bevacizumab is approximately 21 days, so six weeks (42 days) is a suitable timeframe to ensure that most of the drug is cleared from the patient's system before the surgery. This helps to minimize the risk of bleeding complications during the surgical procedure. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Which of the following is a feature of cellular senescence?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following is a feature of cellular senescence?

options.label: A
options.text: Loss of ability to secrete tumorigenic growth factors

questions.solution: Correct Option B - Permanent cell cycle arrest Cellular senescence is irreversible cell cycle arrest. Cellular senescence is a programmed cellular response to significant stress. Cells that are in senescence are unable to divide and there are no known physiologic signals that can stimulate senescent cells to proliferate. However, they remain metabolically active and can continue to secrete mitogens that may promote growth of nearby tumour cells. The cellular membrane remains intact and they do not necessarily undergo apoptosis or necrosis. Senescence occurs when cells experience a potentially "oncogenic stress" that could result in progression to malignancy. Thus, it is a mechanism by which cells attempt to prevent carcinogenesis. Examples of causes include depletion of chromosomal telomeres, accumulated DNA damage, or lack of nutrients. It is dependent on activation of the p53 and Rb proteins, which lead to chromatin modifications preventing necessary gene expression for the G1 to S cell cycle transition. Incorrect Options: Option A - Loss of ability to secrete tumorigenic growth factors: This statement is incorrect. Senescent cells can still secrete various factors, including growth factors, cytokines, and proteases, collectively known as the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP). Some of these factors may have tumor-promoting effects, which is one of the reasons why senescent cells are implicated in aging and cancer. The SASP can promote inflammation and tissue remodeling, which can contribute to tumorigenesis. Option C - Cessation of all metabolic activity: This statement is incorrect. Cellular senescence is not a state of complete metabolic shutdown. Senescent cells remain metabolically active, and they continue to carry out essential cellular functions, although they are no longer capable of dividing. Option D - Loss of cell membrane integrity: This statement is incorrect. Cellular senescence does not involve the loss of cell membrane integrity. Senescent cells remain intact and viable, although they have permanently stopped dividing. They do not undergo cell lysis or disintegration of the cell membrane. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option A - Discharge home and refer for outpatient evaluation: Risk stratification of patients can be performed with the use of a scoring system such as the Glasgow-Blatchford scale to determine which patients are less likely to experience complications of GI bleed and which may need hospital-based therapy. Those patients with a Glasgow-Blatchford score of ≤2 can be safely discharged home. Risk factors include abnormal vital signs that suggest hemodynamic instability, initial hematocrit ≤35%, significant comorbidity, and gross blood on the initial rectal exam. Patients with independent risk factors for severe GI bleeding and adverse outcomes should be diagnosed urgently and should receive focused treatment to improve outcomes. The criteria for the Glasgow Blatchford scale include BUN, hemoglobin, systolic blood pressure, and miscellaneous markers, including tachycardia, melena on presentation, syncope, liver disease, and heart failure. The Rockall scale is another tool for risk. Incorrect Options: Option B - Admit for 24-hour observation: Scores greater than 0 have an increased risk for intervention, and inpatient treatment is recommended. questions.stemHtml: A 25-year-old female with a history of asthma is intubated in the emergency department for acute asthma exacerbation. options.label: A

questions.solution: Correct Option D - Disconnect ventilator: Asthmatic patients can be difficult to manage on the ventilator. They are prone to air-trapping and auto-PEEP, which can lead to hemodynamic collapse. Smaller tidal volumes, lower respiratory rates, and decreased inspiratory:expiratory ratios can minimize this risk. The first step in a decompensating asthmatic patient on the ventilator is to de-connect from the vent and allow any air trapped in the lungs to escape. Often, there is an audible exhalation from the ET tube, and the patient’s hemodynamics will improve. Mnemonic for Troubleshooting Ventilators: D isplacement of ET Tube O bstruction of ET tube P neumothorax E quipment or vent problems S tacked breaths Incorrect Options: Option A - Increasing FiO2 and PEEP: While increasing FiO2 might be helpful in cases of hypoxemia, increasing PEEP in this context could exacerbate the situation. PEEP is used to keep the airways open at the end of expiration, but in a patient with asthma who is already prone to air-trapping, this could lead to an increased intrathoracic pressure, which may further compromise the hemodynamics. Option B - Bolus 2L of NS for volume-depletion: Hypotension can sometimes be due to volume depletion, but in the context of a mechanically ventilated asthmatic patient, the more likely cause of sudden hypotension is increased intrathoracic pressure from air-trapping or a pneumothorax. Aggressive fluid resuscitation won't address these issues and might even complicate management if the patient also has an element of heart failure. Option D - Increase sedation to eliminate auto-PEEPing: While ensuring adequate sedation is important for ventilated patients to ensure patient-ventilator synchrony, it isn't the primary issue in this scenario. Increased sedation won't alleviate the air-trapping that's likely causing this patient's hypotension. Furthermore, over-sedation can lead to its own set of problems, including hemodynamic instability and prolonged ventilator dependence. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 42-year-old female patient comes to your OPD to discuss further management of GERD. She was initially tried on H2-blocker therapy and had an initial response that was then lost. She was subsequently started on PPIs twice daily and has had inadequate symptom improvement. Recent VOGD demonstrates persistent esophagitis but no Barrett’s esophagus or mass lesion. pH studies confirm the presence of GERD. She is frustrated by her remaining symptoms, which have begun to affect her ability to exercise and sleep and her ability to swallow various foods safely. She has also been experiencing worsening regurgitation lately, which was confirmed by a manometry study last month. She asks whether surgery will lead to symptom improvement. Which of the following statements is true regarding anti-reflux surgery in this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 42-year-old female patient comes to your OPD to discuss further management of GERD. She was initially tried on H2-blocker therapy and had an initial response that was then lost. She was subsequently started on PPIs twice daily and has had inadequate symptom improvement. Recent VOGD demonstrates persistent esophagitis but no Barrett’s esophagus or mass lesion. pH studies confirm the presence of GERD. She is frustrated by her remaining symptoms, which have begun to affect her ability to exercise and sleep and her ability to swallow various foods safely. She has also been experiencing worsening regurgitation lately, which was confirmed by a manometry study last month. She asks whether surgery will lead to symptom improvement. Which of the following statements is true regarding anti-reflux surgery in this patient?

options.label: A
options.text: Anti-reflux surgery will eliminate her risk of esophageal cancer.

options.label: B
options.text: Anti-reflux surgery has been shown to improve symptoms in patients with regurgitation.

options.label: C
options.text: Endoluminal antireflux procedures are as effective as anti-reflux surgery without the associated complications of surgery.

options.label: D
options.text: Since she has no evidence of metaplasia or dysplasia on EGD, she is not a candidate for antireflux surgery at this time.

questions.answerText: Anti-reflux surgery has been shown to improve symptoms in patients with regurgitation.
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Anti-reflux surgery has been shown to improve symptoms in patients with regurgitation: Multiple studies have shown that while anti-reflux surgery does help with symptoms in certain patients, it does not alter an individual’s risk for esophageal cancer. Fundoplication should be reserved for patients with proven regurgitation using esophageal manometry studies. Endoscopic anti-reflux procedures including radiofrequency augmentation of the lower esophageal sphincter and endoscopic suturing of the sphincter have not been proven to result in long-term symptom control. Studies have shown that at 3 years after the procedures, patients continued to need medical therapy or a fundoplication procedure. Anti-reflux surgery is contraindicated in patients with metaplasia or dysplasia since it can affect treatment options in case of progression to cancer. Finally, anti-reflux surgery is associated with worsening of dysphagia in some patients; thus, there is no guarantee that her dysphagia will resolve. It is also associated with gas-bloat syndrome and diarrhea. Incorrect Options : Option A - Anti-reflux surgery will eliminate her risk of esophageal cancer: Anti-reflux surgery can reduce the risk of esophageal cancer by effectively controlling acid reflux and reducing inflammation in the esophagus. However, it does not entirely eliminate the risk of esophageal cancer, especially in patients with a long history of GERD and esophagitis. Option C - Endoluminal antireflux procedures are as effective as anti-reflux surgery without the associated complications of surgery: Endoluminal antireflux procedures, such as endoscopic suturing or radiofrequency ablation, are minimally invasive techniques that aim to improve reflux symptoms. While they may be effective in selected cases, they are generally not considered as effective as traditional anti-reflux surgery (fundoplication) for patients with more severe GERD symptoms or those with anatomical abnormalities like hiatal hernia. Option D - Since she has no evidence of metaplasia or dysplasia on EGD, she is not a candidate for antireflux surgery at this time: The presence or absence of metaplasia or dysplasia (Barrett's esophagus) on EGD (Esophagogastroduodenoscopy) is an important factor in determining the risk of esophageal cancer and the need for surveillance. However, it is not the sole factor in deciding whether a patient is a candidate for antireflux surgery. The decision to proceed with surgery should be based on the severity of symptoms, response to medical therapy, and other factors assessed by the treating physician. @Neet_pg_bot

  • Endoscopic anti-reflux procedures including radiofrequency augmentation of the lower esophageal sphincter and endoscopic suturing of the sphincter have not been proven to result in long-term symptom control.

  • Finally, anti-reflux surgery is associated with worsening of dysphagia in some patients; thus, there is no guarantee that her dysphagia will resolve.
  • It is also associated with gas-bloat syndrome and diarrhea.

  • Endoluminal antireflux procedures, such as endoscopic suturing or radiofrequency ablation, are minimally invasive techniques that aim to improve reflux symptoms.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old G1P0 female who is currently 25 weeks pregnant presents to the emergency department with vaginal bleeding and lower abdominal pain. Her vital signs are significant for a blood pressure of 88/52 mm of hg and a heart rate of 122/min. A bedside ultrasound reveals a placental abruption. Laboratory studies indicate a hemoglobin level of 6.7 g/dL, platelets of 70,000/mcL, a prothrombin time (PT) of 33 seconds, a partial thromboplastin time (PTT) of 74 seconds, a creatinine level of 3.4 mg/dL, and an indirect bilirubin of 2.5. A peripheral blood smear reveals many schistocytes. Which of the following is responsible for these abnormalities?
questions.stemHtml: A 27-year-old G1P0 female who is currently 25 weeks pregnant presents to the emergency department with vaginal bleeding and lower abdominal pain. Her vital signs are significant for a blood pressure of 88/52 mm of hg and a heart rate of 122/min. A bedside ultrasound reveals a placental abruption. Laboratory studies indicate a hemoglobin level of 6.7 g/dL, platelets of 70,000/mcL, a prothrombin time (PT) of 33 seconds, a partial thromboplastin time (PTT) of 74 seconds, a creatinine level of 3.4 mg/dL, and an indirect bilirubin of 2.5. A peripheral blood smear reveals many schistocytes. Which of the following is responsible for these abnormalities?
questions.solution: Correct Option D - Release of tissue factor: This patient developed disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) due to a placental abruption . The microangiopathic hemolytic anemia of DIC results from the widespread activation of clotting due to tissue factor activation. The release of tissue factor induces a cascade of intravascular clot formation. These clots contain both platelets and coagulation factors, and patients experience both a hyper and hypocoagulable state. Microvascular fibrin deposition causes ischemic multiorgan dysfunction. Laboratory studies will demonstrate low platelets, low hemoglobin levels (with the presence of schistocytes), and low fibrinogen. Elevations occur in PT/PTT, fibrin degradation products (D-dimers), indirect bilirubin, and creatinine. DIC can accompany a wide range of pathologies including sepsis, trauma, pancreatitis, malignancy, nephrotic syndrome, severe burns, and obstetric complications. Management of DIC is supportive and includes transfusions of packed red blood cells, platelets, fresh frozen plasma, and cryoprecipitate as warranted. The underlying disease must be addressed. Incorrect Options: Option A - Formation of anti-GpIIb/IIIa antibodies: The formation of auto-antibodies to anti-GpIIb/IIIa occurs in immune thrombocytopenia (ITP ). ITP typically results in much lower platelet counts and does not lead to anemia or abnormal coagulation times. Flares may occur during pregnancy in patients who have pre-existing ITP or other autoimmune diseases. Treatment consists of steroids or intravenous immune globulin (IVIG). Option B - Deficiency of ADAMTS13: ADAMTS13 deficiency is the mechanism of thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP ). ADAMTS 13 degrades von Willebrand multimers. When it is deficient, these multimers increase, leading to increased platelet adhesion, aggregation, and subsequently thrombus formation. Similar to DIC, these thrombi cause microangiopathic hemolytic anemia. However, since the clots result from the sole consumption of platelets and not coagulation factors, the prothrombin and partial thromboplastin times are normal. Treatment consists of plasma exchange. Option C - Release of bacterial toxin: Hemolytic uremic syndrome also involves microangiopathic hemolytic anemia. This condition is caused by a shiga-like toxin t hat is released by enterohemorrhagic E. coli. Bloody diarrhea is typical and young children are affected disproportionately. Like TTP, the thrombi are composed solely of platelets. Treatment is supportive. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option A - Group A beta-hemolytic streptococcus and Staphylococcus aureus: The patient's presentation with ill-defined erythema and tenderness progressing rapidly to indurated, dusky, and necrotic skin with bullae and an exudative, malodorous discharge, along with the presence of palpable crepitus, is characteristic of necrotizing fasciitis. Necrotizing fasciitis is a severe soft tissue infection that involves the rapid destruction of fascial planes and surrounding tissues. It is a life-threatening condition that requires immediate and aggressive treatment. Group A beta-hemolytic streptococcus (Streptococcus pyogenes) and Staphylococcus aureus are the most common pathogens responsible for necrotizing fasciitis. These bacteria produce enzymes and toxins that facilitate the rapid spread of infection and tissue destruction. The infection can progress rapidly, leading to sepsis, shock, and organ failure if not treated promptly. Incorrect Options: Option B - Pseudomonas aeruginosa: It is a Gram-negative bacterium that can cause various infections, including wound infections and sepsis. While it can be associated with severe soft tissue infections in certain settings, it is not the most common pathogen responsible for necrotizing fasciitis. Option C - Listeria monocytogenes: It is a Gram-positive bacterium that is often associated with foodborne infections, particularly in immunocompromised individuals and pregnant women. It is not a common cause of necrotizing fasciitis. Option D - Streptococcus bovis: it is a bacterium that has been associated with infective endocarditis, especially in patients with colorectal cancer. While it may cause bacteremia and soft tissue infections, it is not a common pathogen responsible for necrotizing fasciitis. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Which of the following is an FDA-approved medication for the treatment of patients with mild cognitive impairment (also known as very mild dementia)?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following is an FDA-approved medication for the treatment of patients with mild cognitive impairment (also known as very mild dementia)?

options.label: A
options.text: Aducanumab (a monoclonal antibody directed against amyloid-β)

options.label: B
options.text: Axona (a medical food, primarily composed of medium-chain fatty acids)

questions.solution: Correct Option C - Donepezil (an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor): FDA-approved medications for the treatment of Alzheimer disease dementia are limited to cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine), and partial NMDA-receptor antagonists (memantine). Cholinesterase inhibitors are FDA-approved for use in patients with all stages of Alzheimer disease dementia (including very mild dementia; AKA mild cognitive impairment), with clinical trials data establishing a modest benefit in function and cognition in patients with early-stage symptomatic AD dementia (answer option C is therefore correct). Memantine is FDA-approved for the treatment of symptoms associated with moderate-to-severe AD dementia, but not in patients with milder stage disease. Despite multiple trials, there is no evidence that suggests that any approved medications affect underlying progression of disease pathophysiology or exhibits a neuroprotective effect in patients with AD dementia. Aducanumab is a novel monoclonal antibody directed against amyloid-β which is undergoing evaluation in clinical trials. Disease-modifying effects of this medication have not (yet) been established as this medication is not approved for clinical use. Incorrect Options: Option A - Aducanumab (a monoclonal antibody directed against amyloid-β): Aducanumab is an investigational monoclonal antibody that targets amyloid-β, a protein implicated in Alzheimer's disease. As of my knowledge cutoff date in September 2021, aducanumab was undergoing clinical trials and had received attention for potential use in Alzheimer's disease treatment. However, it was not yet FDA-approved for any indication at that time, including mild cognitive impairment (MCI). Option B - Axona (a medical food, primarily composed of medium-chain fatty acids): Axona is a medical food that contains medium-chain triglycerides and is marketed as a dietary option for Alzheimer's disease patients. It is not an FDA-approved medication specifically for mild cognitive impairment (MCI). It is not typically prescribed as a first-line treatment for mild cognitive impairment (MCI), as seen in the scenario. questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman comes to the physician due to a one-month history of weight gain and facial oedema. Her blood pressure is 140/80 mm Hg, her pulse is 80/min, and her examination shows 2+ ankle oedema. Urine analysis shows 3+ proteinuria and fatty casts. Which of the following is most likely the cause of her proteinuria?
questions.stemHtml: A 30-year-old woman comes to the physician due to a one-month history of weight gain and facial oedema. Her blood pressure is 140/80 mm Hg, her pulse is 80/min, and her examination shows 2+ ankle oedema. Urine analysis shows 3+ proteinuria and fatty casts. Which of the following is most likely the cause of her proteinuria?
questions.solution: Correct Option B: Glomerular proteinuria The patient, in this case, has nephrotic syndrome. Nephrotic syndrome is a clinical syndrome characterized by the following: Proteinuria (> 3-3.5 g/day - most important manifestation) Hypoalbuminemia Edema Hyperlipidemia and lipiduria The basic pathology is the altered permeability of the glomerular membrane for proteins. Diseases most commonly causing nephrotic syndrome are: Minimal change disease (in children) Membranous glomerulopathy (adults) Mesangial proliferative glomerulonephritis Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis Proteinuria is excessive protein excretion in the urine, generally greater than 150 mg daily in adults. Proteinuria can be associated with high serum creatinine levels, elevated blood urea nitrogen (BUN) or evidence of systemic illness (e.g., fever, rash, vasculitis). Glomerular proteinuria is a medical condition characterized by excess protein in the urine due to abnormalities in the glomerular filtration barrier in the kidneys. The glomerular filtration barrier is a complex structure comprising three layers: the fenestrated endothelium, the basement membrane, and the podocytes. This barrier is responsible for filtering out waste products and excess fluid from the blood while preventing larger molecules, such as proteins, from entering the urine. Glomerular proteinuria can occur when there is damage or disruption to any of these layers, which can lead to the passage of protein into the urine. It results from the effacement of epithelial cell foot processes and altered glomerular permeability with an increased filtration fraction of normal plasma proteins, as in diabetic nephropathy. Protein electrophoresis will have a pattern exhibiting a large albumin spike indicative of the increased permeability of albumin across the damaged GBM. Incorrect options: Option A: Functional proteinuria Functional proteinuria is not due to any underlying disease or medical condition but a functional body response to certain stressors. This type of proteinuria is usually benign and self-limiting and does not require any specific treatment. Functional proteinuria can be caused by a variety of factors, including: Exercise Fever Emotional stress Dehydration Functional proteinuria is a benign process resulting from acute illness, exercise, and "orthostatic proteinuria." Orthostatic proteinuria usually causes protein excretion of less than 1 g/day. It occurs only during the daytime and is associated with an upright posture. This patient has a history of nephrotic syndrome, so functional proteinuria is unlikely. Option C: Tubular proteinuria Tubular proteinuria is a medical condition characterized by excess protein in the urine due to abnormalities in the reabsorption of proteins by the tubular cells in the kidneys. Normally, the kidney tubular cells reabsorb small amounts of protein that pass through the glomeruli and into the filtrate. However, in tubular proteinuria, there is a defect in the tubular cells that impairs their ability to reabsorb proteins, leading to increased protein levels in the urine. It occurs as the reabsorption of normally filtered proteins in the proximal tubule is defective. It occurs due to a variety of causes: Acute tubular necrosis Toxic injury (lead, aminoglycosides and certain antiretrovirals), Drug-induced interstitial nephritis Hereditary metabolic disorders (Wilson disease and Fanconi syndrome). Option D: Overload proteinuria Overload proteinuria is a medical condition characterized by excess protein in the urine due to abnormal blood proteins that exceed the renal tubules' reabsorptive capacity. In this type of proteinuria, the excess protein is not due to a defect in the glomerular filtration barrier or tubular reabsorption but rather due to an excess of abnormal proteins that the renal tubules cannot properly reabsorb. Overload proteinuria can result from: Overproduction of circulating, filterable plasma proteins (monoclonal gammopathies), such as Bence Jones proteins associated with plasma cell myeloma (formerly multiple myeloma). Correct Option B: Glomerular proteinuria

  • The patient, in this case, has nephrotic syndrome. 
  • Nephrotic syndrome is a clinical syndrome characterized by the following:
    • Proteinuria (> 3-3.5 g/day - most important manifestation)
    • Hypoalbuminemia
    • Edema
    • Hyperlipidemia and lipiduria
  • The basic pathology is the altered permeability of the glomerular membrane for proteins. 
  • Diseases most commonly causing nephrotic syndrome are:
    • Minimal change disease (in children)
    • Membranous glomerulopathy (adults)
    • Mesangial proliferative glomerulonephritis
    • Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis
    • Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis
  • Proteinuria is excessive protein excretion in the urine, generally greater than 150 mg daily in adults.
  • Proteinuria can be associated with high serum creatinine levels, elevated blood urea nitrogen (BUN) or evidence of systemic illness (e.g., fever, rash, vasculitis).
  • Glomerular proteinuria is a medical condition characterized by excess protein in the urine due to abnormalities in the glomerular filtration barrier in the kidneys. 
  • The glomerular filtration barrier is a complex structure comprising three layers: the fenestrated endothelium, the basement membrane, and the podocytes. 
  • This barrier is responsible for filtering out waste products and excess fluid from the blood while preventing larger molecules, such as proteins, from entering the urine.
  • Glomerular proteinuria can occur when there is damage or disruption to any of these layers, which can lead to the passage of protein into the urine.
  • It results from the effacement of epithelial cell foot processes and altered glomerular permeability with an increased filtration fraction of normal plasma proteins, as in diabetic nephropathy. 
  • Protein electrophoresis will have a pattern exhibiting a large albumin spike indicative of the increased permeability of albumin across the damaged GBM.

  • Functional proteinuria is not due to any underlying disease or medical condition but a functional body response to certain stressors.
  • This type of proteinuria is usually benign and self-limiting and does not require any specific treatment.
  • Functional proteinuria can be caused by a variety of factors, including:
    • Exercise 
    • Fever
    • Emotional stress 
    • Dehydration 
  • Functional proteinuria is a benign process resulting from acute illness, exercise, and "orthostatic proteinuria." 
  • Orthostatic proteinuria usually causes protein excretion of less than 1 g/day.
  • It occurs only during the daytime and is associated with an upright posture.
  • This patient has a history of nephrotic syndrome, so functional proteinuria is unlikely. 

Option C: Tubular proteinuria

  • Tubular proteinuria is a medical condition characterized by excess protein in the urine due to abnormalities in the reabsorption of proteins by the tubular cells in the kidneys. 
  • Normally, the kidney tubular cells reabsorb small amounts of protein that pass through the glomeruli and into the filtrate. However, in tubular proteinuria, there is a defect in the tubular cells that impairs their ability to reabsorb proteins, leading to increased protein levels in the urine.

  • It occurs due to a variety of causes: 
    • Acute tubular necrosis
    • Toxic injury (lead, aminoglycosides and certain antiretrovirals), 
    • Drug-induced interstitial nephritis 
    • Hereditary metabolic disorders (Wilson disease and Fanconi syndrome).

  • Overload proteinuria is a medical condition characterized by excess protein in the urine due to abnormal blood proteins that exceed the renal tubules' reabsorptive capacity.

    • Amyloidosis: Amyloidosis is a condition in which abnormal proteins build up in various tissues in the body, including the kidneys, and can lead to overflow proteinuria.
    • Sickle cell disease: Sickle cell disease can cause the breakdown of red blood cells, releasing hemoglobin into the blood and urine, leading to overflow proteinuria.
    • Fabry disease: It is a genetic disorder in which a buildup of a specific type of fat in the body can produce abnormal proteins that can be excreted in the urine, leading to overflow proteinuria.
  • Protein electrophoresis from the serum or urine will exhibit a discrete protein peak.
  • Other examples of overload proteinuria include myoglobinuria in rhabdomyolysis and hemoglobinuria in hemolysis.
